MR. SMITH : Interview with Baby Lovett, being interviewed by Art Smith, and this is side one of tape one. Also after the After Hours where we've all played many, many times, it's quiet here this is why we're here now. It seemed like an appropriate place for an interview. Assisting in the interview is Charles "Crook" Goodwin, a friend of Baby's for well over 40 years. Crook is also a member of the Art Smith Kansas City Jazz Band and been there since the band was formed 12 years ago.

We'd like to start this interview now with Mr. Samuel "Baby" Lovett by asking him about his early childhood; where he was born and how he moved up here to Kansas City. Baby, as I understand it you were born in Pineville, Louisiana. Tell us about your childhood and your parents, and whatever you think is of interest.

Well, I was born in Pineville, Louisiana and I came to Alexandria, Louisiana when I was a very, very young man. And I moved from Alexandria, Louisiana to Shreveport, Louisiana, and I had a job in Shreveport at the Star Theatre, Texas Avenue. And I was there for I guess about eight years all together, playing with a fine band and I left --
when I left the theatre I started playing with different bands around in Kansas City. And I --
What year would that be, Baby?
In Shreveport that was in the thirties. No, twenties, it was in the twenties, in the twenties, it was in the twenties.
What year did you come to Kansas City?
That was in '24. And I've been here ever since. I had a job, my first big job was at the Eblon Theatre on Vine Street, between 18th and 19th.
What kind of a theatre was that?
The Eblon.
No, what kind was it? Silent movies?
Silent movies.
Were you in the pit band there?
(Inaudible) silent movies.
Who was playing with you in that pit band?

Well, I can't remember all the guys names, but I know one was Guy O. Taylor was one. And Socks Mokin was two. And (inaudible) a trombone player. And Guy Taylor was the violin player, a wonderful musician. He had the band there, see. And he had a bass player by the name of Eppy Jackson.
This was like about 1924.
Yeah. And Eppy was one of the greatest
tuba players I've ever met in my life. He played a tuba like you play a trumpet. And so then our piano player was named Scott, and then after Scott passed, Basie, Count Basie.
Count Basie joined the band. What, on the organ?
Yes.
In this pit band of the silent movies.
That's right. And --
What can you tell us about Basie when he was playing with your band?

Well, Basie never played -- he hadn't been on organ very long, you understand what I mean? You know, organs are very loud instruments which everybody knows you put one finger on there and run everybody out of town. So they had one of those pictures where a guy was slipping up on a woman, you understand what I mean, with a knife, fixing to cut her, you know. And it was quiet in there, you know, it's quiet in there and everybody's wondering what will happen. And Basie let out on an organ, man, playing the blues. And I touched Basie on the shoulder and said, hey, play (inaudible). It was a kind of tragedy, like, you know, . . . (inaudible) I said play an old number (singing of notes). And he laughed. And he started right again, man, playing the blues.
I told him, you know, -- I was in front of the band, I told him, I said, I think I'm going to have to let you

go, man, you don't seem to understand that -- he said, okay, don't bother me now, I'll get it. I said, okay, man, but next time I want to hear the down side, and so I didn't have any more trouble, at the Eblon.

And I left there. I played -- it was 12th Street then, they played at 12th Street in the nightclub called Ben Payne Jazzland, upstairs you know. We had a woman bouncer, you know, she weighed about 200. If a guy get tough in there man, you know, she'd take him and throw him down the steps. And from there let's see, I went to -- I'm trying to figure where did I go to after I left.
Was it the Pompey Room?
Yeah, Pompey Room downtown. And I stayed there for quite a while.
Would that be up into the late twenties?
Yes, in the late twenties. I went down there and they had an explosion at the theatre there then.
Oh, that's when you went to the Gillis Theatre.
Yeah, the Gillis.
What year was that, the late twenties or early thirties?
This was the twenties.
The twenties. Gillis -- yes, it seems to me I read about that. What happened there any way?

Well, any way they had a little hamburger joint right around the stand, right around the corner there, and the piano player and I, [Harris Wanigan,] we went around to this little hamburger joint. We started around there, as soon as we got into the lobby this explosion went off, man. Well, what happened, it was kind of misty rain that day -- that night, I mean, and I thought I was running up fast, you know, and I fell man, on the street with all that water, you know. You understand what I mean. Somebody said, I don't know who it was, oh, Baby's dead. And you talk about a guy scrambling man, I was -- I had mud all over me. So I came out of that all right. We stayed there for a long time.
You had a long stay at the Gillis. Well, of course you didn't go back to the Gillis Theatre.
No, no.
After the fire. Tell me where did you meet Tilly, your beautiful wife, who is such a magnificent lady.
Oh, Alexandria, Louisiana.
Oh, you met her down south and brought her to Kansas City with you.
That's right.
She's certainly a favorite person of all of us.
We I started sweethearing with her when I was 13 years old.
Oh, man, fabulous, fabulous. Well, we all miss her greatly, and I know you do.
Oh, yes. We were together 55 years.
That's a long time.
A long time.

Well, now, it's the late twenties in the Gillis Theatre, what were some of the other -- from there -- here in Kansas City things really started to go, didn't they, in the 1930s, in the early thirties. You really -- you weren't out of work very much, or any other musicians were you?
Oh, no. We wasn't making any money amounting to anything.
Tell me about the money. How were you paid?
We would play 9:00 o'clock until 5:00 in the morning off the Spinnin' Wheel (Inaudible). And your highest payment was $2.50 --
A night.
-- a night, yeah.
And you played for tips I guess mostly.
That's right, tips were great, though.
Were they?

Yeah. And they were awful nice to us you understand, because we played all the stuff. And Basie was right down the street at the Reno Arena then, and during the intermission I'd go down and see Basie, when he'd have an inter-
mission he'd come to see me.
Great.
That's what we used to do. And let's see, after I left there -- I came to the Rialto, I think.
The Rialto?
Yeah, Rialto Theatre, yeah, 18th and Hyland.
What was that in the pit band there, or were you all part of the stage?
Yeah, pit band, yeah. Emil Williams playing piano.
Who was playing piano?
Emil Williams.
Emil Williams?
Yeah.
Anybody else in that band we should know about?
Well, I didn't -- let's see. Goobie, his real name was Guy Taylor. He was a violinist.
Really fine.
Oh, yes. And --

Well, I'm going to get to the personalities later on, Baby, but I thought, you know, when you mentioned Basie at the Eblon Theatre, and him playing a blues when he's supposed to be playing that sneaky type music for a

silent thing, I thought it belonged in there. But we're going to get to all the people later on, but I'm interested, you know, I think we're all interested in the sort of sequence of events right up to today because I know what was happening just recently. You and I were playing around the corner from each- other when you were at Huck Finns and we were at Vitale's Batelly's Vil- lage Gate.
That's right.

But inbetween now from the Rialto where did you go? And if you can sort of the years, you know, early thirties, '32, '33. You see, we skipped -- you were born in 1894 and we're already up to the early thirties. Charles, did you have something you wanted to say?

Yeah. In the early thirties Baby Lovett and I were playing together in a band called Thaman Hayes. Now, this was a band that was made up of us fellas who were recently with George Lee's band, Baby Lovett was from George Lee's band, he had started playing with George Lee, right after he left the Rialto Theatre.

Wait, we're jumping ahead a little bit. That's one of the bands I want to cover in detail, that band. Let's see, we haven't even discussed George Lee yet, and he came before Thaman Thayman Hayes, right?
Right.
Well, see, we haven't even discussed

George Lee yet. I want him to get a broad, chronological sequence up to today and then we're going to go back over these people in much more detail. So you left the Rialto and then you went where, approximately, you know, I mean there are so many rooms I know that you played.
I think I left there and went to the Eblon.
No, you were at the Eblon before that, you said.
I'm trying to think, I think I'm getting it straight now. It was so far back.
We've gotten two things confused. He was at the Pompey Room before the Avalon was in existence. See, the Avalon just opened about 1923 and you were in the Pompey Room before then.
So he came to Kansas City before 1923.
Had to.
Had to.
Because the Avalon didn't open until about -- late 1923.
In '22 when I came here.
Well, that would be right. Well, thank you, Crook.
Well, any way, the sequence may be a little bit changed but you were working -- you had no trouble getting jobs
in those years of the twenties and into the thirties.
No, no.
And you brought Tilly up here with you. Where did you -- of course you own your own home now here on Olive Street, did you -- where did you live when you first came here, you and Tilly?
Tenth Street. Rooming over there. From there to where I am now.
Out Olive Street, you've been out there. You know, I often wondered how you got around because you never drive a car, I've never seen you drive a car, Baby, in all the years we've known you.
Well, I never did --
Learn to drive.
-- learn to drive, no.
But you always got a ride when you had to play.
That's right. And still doing that.

Now, we're up to the thirties -- well, the late twenties. At that time -- up until that time did you ever get a chance to go out of town with a band and travel with a band, up to say 1930. Did you travel at all?
Not -- very little.
Very little.
Yeah, very little.
Not enough to mention. Maybe into Denver or Chicago or Omaha or something like that.
Omaha, yeah. Went there quite often.
Yeah. All right, now we're into the early thirties and you and Tilly -- when did you go to Olive Street and buy that house, you and Tilly? Early thirties was it?
Well, let me see. Yeah, I think that was in the thirties.
Yeah.
Yeah, thirties.
And you worked out of there all the time and played all these gigs. Were you -- you were with George Lee for a long time, and Julia Lee.
Oh, yes.
You probably spent more time when that band than any other band.
That's right, yeah. That's right.
What -- I'm just going to make sure that we get back to George and Julia Lee, but I just want to get this chronology down first. What years were you with George Lee?
That was back in --
Well, you were with him a lot of years.
What span did that cover?
Let's see, I think that was about in the twenties, around about '25 or '26.
Until when?
I was with George around about five years, I think.
Is that all?
Yeah.
Five years. So that would up until 1931.
That's right.
Is that when you started out with your own band or did you join some other band. No, that would be about the time you went with Thamon Hayes.
Right.
You left George Lee to go with Thamon Hayes.
Right.

That terrific, tremendous band. I just read an article on Thamon Hayes' band and the headline was "the Kansas City band that fame just eluded." And I think that was a wonderful title for that article. We're going to get back to that band. Now you went with Thamon Hayes in about '31, '32. '31. Now, how long were you with that band?
Well, I was with them about -- let me
see, I guess about three or four years. About three years. Well, you went to Chicago with them I guess when they went up there. Twice.
Twice.
All right, that takes you up to '34, '35, and then what happened when you left Thamon Hayes' great band?
Let's see now, where did I go? It's been quite a while now back. How are we doing?
Well, we're getting up to the present, we're only 40 years away.
Spinning Wheel.
Oh, yes, I've heard so much about that room.
Did you have your own band or were you with someone else?
Yeah, I had my own band.
Who was on that band, do you remember?
Woody Walder.
Woody Walder.
Yeah. Herman Walder.
And Herman Walder. Herman's with me now, has been for years.
Booker Washington.
Booker. He's been with me for 12 years.
And Joshua Jones.
Oh, Josh, right, may God rest his soul. Marvelous pianist.
That was a terrific band you had there. Oh, man, we could play there. From 9:00 o'clock until 5:00 in the morning.
Six nights a week?
Yeah. I was the leader, I'd get two and a half a night and they'd get a dollar and a half.
Those were the days, huh?

Oh, sure. And everybody in the band would drink, you understand what I mean. There was an Italian fella running the Spinning Wheel, and he had a big can, he'd bring us beer in a can, you know, spike it with alcohol. And man, before we'd leave there everybody was high.
Jelly Roll Morton used to call him the can rusher.
Oh, yeah. I can't say this one.
Sure you can. Please do.

Anyway, they had a little hamburger joint right on the corner of the Spinning Wheel, you know, and we'd get off right about 5:00 o'clock in the morning, man, and I stopped there one night bought some limburger cheese, and -- I mean a hamburger, made a sandwich of it, you understand

what I mean? And I ate an onion on top of it man and went home. My wife asked me, said -- I smoked one of those Italian cigars, they're strong man. And my wife woke me up around 6:00 or 7:00 o'clock in the morning, I said what's the matter she said you too far up in the bed? Now, listen she's smelling that limburger cheese. Oh, man, that was something.
Yeah, that was when everyone was young.
Yeah.
Full of pep, vim and vigor. So you were at the Spinning Wheel for three or four years.
Yeah.
It was back in the thirties, I know. That must have been about --
About 1936.
Yeah.
And then where did you go from there, Baby?
From the Spinning Wheel I went with Julia Lee.
Oh. What had happened to George, had he died?
No, he wasn't --
What did they do split up, George and
Yeah. Well, I was with George and Julia for a while.
Yeah, but that's before you went with Thamon Thaymond Hayes.
Yes.
Just one second. Yes, Crook.

The way I remember it after Lovett left George Lee's band the band became a seven or eight piece band, it wasn't a big band any more. If you'll remember. And then Julia left the band. After Thaymond Thamon Hayes you got with Julia as a duo, just Julia and you.
That's right.
And you were -- I think your first job with Julia was out at Milton's.
Milton's on --
Milton's Taproom Tavern on 35th.
Well, where does this band come in that was at the Spinning Wheel?
This was after Thaymond's Thamon's band.
After Thaymond's Thamon's band then he -- then Spinning Wheel then after the Spinning Wheel he went with Julia Lee out to Milton's on Main Street, which is still there. Right.
Right.

Now weren't you -- at Milton's right. That -- I've heard so much about you and Julia there,everybody -- I mean, any person who's lived in this city for any length of time at all remembers you and Julia at Milton's. You must have been there quite a while.
Yeah, I was there quite a while out at Milton's. A long time.
Over 12 years, I would guess, from --
Yeah, 12 years until about --
Just the two of you?
Just the two of us, yes.
She was marvelous, wasn't she? You cut some records with her, I believe.
Oh, yes.
In fact I think I've heard some, in fact I think I bought some years ago when I first came here.
// King Sized Papa // was the name of one of them.
// King Sized Papa. //
Right.
What were some of the others you did, can you remember?
Well, that's about all I can remember now. It's a long time, you know, but I remember that number.
Everybody speaks very well of her.
Oh, she was wonderful. And we -- Milton didn't have to pay us many times, you know. We had a big kitty there, you know, and we'd make our salary in the kitty. He didn't have to pay us a lot of times.
He never did?
No. We split 90, $100.00, you know, a piece.
Yeah.
Yeah.
And Milton got the music for nothing.
That's right.

Well, we've got them -- George and Julia Lee to talk about a little later. Now this brings us up into the early forties, and then when Julia died, didn't she? What happened -- did you and Julia split up in the forties?
Late forties, yeah.
Late forties. You were with her all the time until the late forties, just the two of you, at Milton's.
That's right.
Well, you were doing so well, what made you split up, you know, why did you split up with Julia?
Well, I don't know. We were off for a while and then she got a job in I think it was the Cuban Room.
And she was --
So you had to go look for a job for yourself.
Yeah, she was doing the single up there.
She was doing a single. Then what did you -- when she got that job where did you go to work? Did you form a band of your own?
Yes.
Where did you go?
Around town here, we would play on the highway and everything, you know.
Well, who was on that band?
On the highway. Let's see, I'll tell you, I can't --
Well, Charles will remember. Yes, Crook.

Gene Carter, tenor sax, and I remember two saxophone players you had. Clayburn Graves was one of them and Gene Carter. They were at different times, though. You used both of them. You was out to the New Forty Inn they called it, out on 40 Highway. You remember it?
Yes.
And--
Who did he have on piano? Was Joshua
No. It wasn't Joshua, it was --
Sleepy?
I can't -- no. Let's see, Joshua was with me on the highway there, you know.
That was Gene that was playing with you. Do you remember.
Did you have a trumpet on that band?
No, we didn't have a trumpet.
Any way, it must have been about this time that you got the call from Basie, wasn't it, to go to New Jersey?
Later.
Later? I thought it was the late forties.
It was later,yeah.
What year did you go east to join Basie's band?
That was in about '32.
No, no, no, it had to be much later than that.
No, wait a minute.
Wait a minute. Yeah, that was in '42.
Well, see, we're out of sequence now.
In other words we're up to the late forties, out on highway 40,
but you didn't mention going with Basie in '42. Where were you playing when you left to go with Basie and with whom were you playing?
I don't think I was working any place when Basie called.
What did you do get a telegram or a letter.
Yeah, yeah.
You got a telegram.
Yeah. He wired me. Macey O'Burch wired me, Basie's booker.
Oh, yeah.
His manager.
Who was his manager.
Macey O'Burch.
Macey O'Burch?
Yeah, he was booking Basie then.

Uh-huh. And he wired you to join the band in New Jersey. We're going to come back to that. I'm trying to get these things in sequence, you know, first, and then we'll go back to the specifics of various people and orchestras and so on. Now, we're out on highway 40 with Gene Carter on saxophone, and this is about what year? Late forties? '41. Oh, we haven't got into the late forties. '41, then '42. All right, and how long were you with Basie?
About six weeks.
Six weeks.
Right.
And then you came back to Kansas City.
Right.
What did Jo' Jones rejoin the band?
Yes. Jo -- when he sent for me, Jo were ill at the time, you know, and he sent for me.
And you filled in for Jo.
And I -- without any rehearsal or anything.

Well, we're going to get to the details of that. I know, I heard -- you know, you told me so much about it years ago. You know, Crook, Baby Lovett was the first musician friend I made in this city when I moved here in 1962. He introduced me to all of you, my old band.
(Inaudible).
That's when I met you.
That's right, my old band. You introduced me to every member of that band, and we've been together ever since.
Sure have.
I hope you don't think you made any mistakes, Baby.
No, I don't think I made any.
But I remember, you know, at your house

listening to your records and going through your scrapbook, and eating that wonderful food that Tilly prepared, and just enjoying myself so much. It's been too long ago, really. I'm talking about like 10 years ago.
That's right.
But any way, you were with Basie's band in 1942 for about six weeks, and then Jo Jones came back on the band, and you came back to Kansas City.
That's right.
And what did you do, did you get a job with another band when you came back? I suppose you rested for a while.
I rested for a while, I didn't go right to work when I came back. No. Let me see --but the toughest thing for me was to sit in Jo's at Jules' seat, and he'd play his drums, you know.
You were using his drums?
No rehearsal or nothing. The music was right on his tom-toms.
The tom-tom, the floor at tom-tom.
And yeah, I had to look at that music man you know, watch the band and all that.
I know it must have been rough.
Oh, man. It was all right as long as the curtain was down, you know. I knew 'One O'clock Jump,'
that was Basie's theme song. I knew that, I think I played that one good, you know. But while that was playing the curtain was going up, man, and boy, it was just packed, the place was just packed.
Right.
And that's the first time I ever got real excited man, and all of those people looked like one to me out there, you know.
I know, I've been through it, I've been through it, I know. It's one blur out there.
Yeah, man. When I got through with that, Peg Leg Bates was on.
He was one of the acts?
Yeah, he was on -- and Maxine Sullivan.
Oh, marvelous, beautiful singer.
Oh, yeah, man --
I saw her not too long ago with the World's Greatest Jazz Band. She's great. She's beautiful today. Her hair's white, you know.
Yeah.
But her face is still as young as ever. But she was one of the acts too. She wasn't with the band, I don't think she ever sang.
No, she wasn't with the band.
She was one of the acts.
Yeah, one of the acts. And Peg Leg Bates Base, you know, and he --
And you had to play all that music to back these people up.
Oh, man, you've got to read man. If you don't read, (--) I'll tell you that, you've got to read,

Right. Well, Baby, I want to come back to those -- to that six weeks with Basie, and to your other experiences, and we're up to about 1942. I want to change the tape and we'll pick up when you came back to Kansas City.
Okay.
This is the end of side one of tape one.
(Side 2)

Interview with Samuel Baby Lovett for the National Endowment for Arts of the Smithsonian Institution. On side one of this tape one we got up to 1942, where Baby has spent six weeks with Count Basie back east and now he has returned to Kansas City. And he was taking things easy for a while and now, Baby, what did you do next when you went back to work? With whom, or do you form your own band, and where did you go after you left Basie?
I came back to Kansas City.
Exactly
Well, But I rested for a long time. I had
to take my rest.
Was it a voluntary rest or was it because you couldn't find work?
Well, voluntary. I was worn out you know, I just had to have a rest.
That was a tough six weeks.
Yeah. It was when I had that pneumonia.
Oh, I didn't know you had pneumonia.
Sure.
When you came back from Basie's band?
No, this is --
No, I'm talking about 1942.
Yes, Baby. What happened when you came back?
I rested a while.
Yeah, and then what did you do?
Well, I don't know the first job I had it's been so long, back, I don't know exactly who I worked with. It's been a long time.
Charles, do you remember?

I believe that then Baby had formed a band and was working on 40 Highway. This was after you come back from Basie. I really remember it because I was in the service in '42 and '43 I got out. When I got out in '43

Now this gentleman you heard speaking is Charles Crook Goodwin who's been a friend of Baby Lovett's for over 40 years and who has been on the Art Smith Kansas City Jazz Band for over 12. He's presently the lead vocalist and guitarist with the Art Smith Kansas City Jazz Band. He was Charles Crook Goodwin. Now Crook brings you out to Highway 40, around 1943. So who were you with there, was it your own band or were you with another band, what was the name of the room?
I had the new 40 Inn.
The new 40 Inn.
Yeah. I had my own band.
Do you remember who was on that band?
I can't remember. It's hard for me to remember. That was a long time. I forgot who was playing piano with me then.
Was Booker on the band or Herman or Art -- no, it wouldn't be Art.
No, no. Oh, long time. I can't remember that. Too far back for me.
Well, how long were you out there, Baby?
Well, I was out on the highway there for about -- let's see, I guess about four, three or four months. It wasn't too long.
Then where did you go?
I didn't --
Did you keep the band organized?
Yeah, the band was still organized but we were off for quite a while after I left there. And we wasn't doing anything because we needed the rest any way, the whole band.

Well, at some point you went to Washington to play for President Truman's Inauguration Ball. Now that would have been in the mid-forties. Now what band was that you brought with you and where were you playing when you brought them to Washington?
Only Julia Lee and myself.
That was just Julia Lee that you two got together for that.
Yes. They asked us to come.
Oh, I'm sure they did. Yeah, you played for President Truman's Inauguration.
That's right.
Charles, did you want to say something?
What I was going to say is Julia and Lovett went to Washington, D.C. They were invited by the president.
Yeah, I know.
Harry Truman.
Yeah, we know this, but were they together before they went there, did they just get together for this gig in Washington?
Oh, they were together --
Oh, we were together before then.
Well, I know you'd worked for years but then you left. You see, I'm trying to get it in a chronological sequence. You'd already told me you had left Julia Lee.
Yeah, she started at the Cuban Room. That was before.
Oh, the inauguration was before they split.
Yeah.
Oh, I see. So you were with Julia Lee when you went with Basie. You left Julia to go back east is that so?
That's right.

Now we're getting it straight. So then you came back and you went back with Julia Lee because if you were with Basie in '42 and you went to the inauguration what, in '45? Or -- Roosevelt didn't die until '45, for Christ's sake. Truman wasn't inaugurated President until Roosevelt died and then he won the election in '48. Okay, so about '45, right.
Yeah.
This was when President Truman took over when President Roosevelt died. This was not the inauguration of 1948 when President Truman won that big election.
No, no.
This was in 1945.
All right.
So you were still with Julia Lee then.
That's right.
Okay. After the inauguration where were you, at Milton's.
Yes.
I see. And how long were you at Milton's with Julia?
Well, I guess about -- let's see, maybe about three or four years, not too long, it wasn't too long, or five years. Not over five.

-- of President Truman, then you came back. I would think it would be closer to seven years you were together at Milton's.

At the Sterling Club?

Well, any way, from there did you keep

Well, you know --
Every time I turn around you were working in a different room and I wish I got the booking instead of you, you know, even today.
You know, some of the best cats were off, man. Benny Goodman and everybody else.
Oh, everybody gets off, I know that. You can't work all the time. Unfortunately -- so what is the next gig that you remember after the Sterling Club?
After the Sterling Club? Oh, man.
It would be the late forties.
It's hard for me to remember way back then.
We're getting pretty close, it's only 25, 26 years.
After the Sterling Club -- did I tell you I was with Julia before then?

Yeah. That band didn't last too long I know that. But I don't remember just what happened after that. I know I was off for a while.

Fifties.

Yeah.

Sure.

Well, I -- my brother started me.
What was his name?
James Lovett. We called him Bud for you know --
You called him Bud.

That's right. He taught me how to play. Well, I -- he didn't teach me but I could hear him practicing at home there, you know, and he has fine drums, had his fine drums set up. Man, I'd get me a lard bucket and go out and --
A lard bucket?
Yeah, lard bucket. And some chair around and -- any kind of stick I could find, see, and I'd hear
him make something on his and I'd try to make it on my cans.
Outdoors.
Outdoors, yeah.
On that bucket.
He used to tell me to stop, I'd say okay. When I was thinking about it he told me to stop, so that's the way I learned.
And do you remember your first set of drums, your first real set of drums. What kind were they?
Duplex.
Duplex.
Yeah.

Oh, big bass drums, yeah. Because it was hard to see me back there.
Where did you get that one when you moved to Shreveport I guess, huh?
Yeah.
You moved across the river to Shreveport.
Uh-huh.
Or to Alexandria.
To Alexandria.
Yeah, Louisiana. Is that where you got the drums, your first set? Did you get them there or up in
I got them in Alexandria.
Alexandria.
Duplex. They sure was fine drums.

Oh, they had good cymbals.
Did they?
But they had those swinging pedals, you know.
Yeah.
You know swinging pedals, did you ever see those?
No, I never did see those one.
Is that right?
No. What did this pedal do?
Yeah, that was something, man.

It was about -- the way they're making them now.
Just about that? Six inches.
Yeah, Duplex was it.
Duplex was the name of your drums, that first drum set.
Yeah, makes no difference how damp the weather is, man, they're still sharp, they still stay sharp. I've never seen nothing like that before.
What?
These drum heads.

Then.
Then. Well, they were all skin then, weren't they?
Yeah, all skin.

Yeah, plastic, yeah.

What do you mean?
Your drums.
Drums.

Rogers is the last one, yeah.
Because you changed them a lot, you know.
Yeah, my drums are not so great now, it's not an expensive drum at all. So --
Well, every time I've ever seen you play it's always been a great set.

Well, what stopped me man from trying to have those fine drums was when I was in Alexandra, Louisiana, you know, and everybody, 'Baby Lovett's the greatest drummer in the world,' you know. All the show girls and all that, so my head got kind of big, you know. And then what stopped me from bragging, man, there was a little cat that came in there in Alexandra, and I was --
(Recording interruption)

That's what everybody said, greatest in the world they said, you know. And I thought I were really great, so don't -- that learned me a lesson, don't never brag. Just keep your mouth shut, and watch the guys that play the same instrument that you play doesn't talk very much, boy. Don't fool with him.
What happened to you?

What happened, man, is those little cats I was playing at the Star Theatre, Shreveport, Louisiana. The Whitman Sisters was there, you remember them, all pretty girls. And I was -- Alice was my girl friend and I thought I was a pimp, she bought me with silk shirts and all that kind of stuff, man. So I'm living right back of the theatre, I can walk out of the theatre into my house, you know, about (inaudible) back there. And oh, they were there man, I was trying to show off, man. You know, they

had xylophones and all that stuff, playin' em piano man and a little guy just stood there and watched me I guess about a half hour just standing looking at me, just play like that. I said, man what is the guy watching me for, you understand what I mean? So we had intermission see, and he asked me, he said, would you mind -- he said my name is Jesse Aiken, what might be your name. I said Baby Lovett, so what. I was supposed to be great, you know.

Then we played, had another intermission, he's still standing there looking at me, and then he asked me, this is the way he approached me. 'Would you mind if I beat a piece fine drums s***n' up there, xylophones and all that stuff, on your drum?' I said, sure, man, (inaudible) That cat played so much drum, man, I walked out the back. I walked out the back, I told my wife I was sick. And she said you'd better go in there and take your medicine, or something like that. I said, I've got a headache, you know. The cat, man, he scared me. That cat could play, man. I never did see him any more. That was all to it. I never did see that cat any more, man. So don't ever think that you're great.
Well, we all learn that the hard way, we all learned it pretty much like that.
I'm telling you man. Never think that you're great.

Yeah, Julia and myself.

That's right.

Well, -- Benny Carter.

Yeah, he --

Yeah, he was living there.

Yeah, yeah.

Yeah, we had to make the band --

Well, we had --
Oh, you recorded in a studio, right?
Dickenson made a--

Yeah. They made a recording with us. Nick and -- oh, I can't think of all the guys. About five or six of us. But some of the guys I didn't even know and I can't even think of their names now, man.
Yeah. But that was in the studio in
Los Angeles.
That's right.
Those were great --
For Capitol.

Yeah, Capitol. That would be in the mid-forties, wouldn't it? About '46, '47. It seems to me I've seen write ups in jazz anthologies referring to Baby and Julia out there with Benny Carter and Vic Dickenson.
It was back in the forties.
Do you remember where you stayed when you were in California making those records?
Yeah, I stayed at the Clark Hotel.
The Clark Hotel. Did Julia stay there too?
Yeah.

And you left Tilly back here in Kansas City.
Yeah.
Tilly is Mrs. Lovett who recently passed on, whom we all miss greatly. Well, how did you enjoy yourself in California on a record date? Did you play any gigs while you were there?
No.
No. You just went out there to record.

Did you get a good contract from Capitol?
Yeah, nice.
Everything was fine.
Yeah, oh, yeah. Dave Dexter.
Dave Dexter, did he produce it?
Oh,yeah.
Oh, you had a good man.

Charles Crook Goodwin.

In New York?
Yeah.

Oh, yeah.

At the theatre there.
At the Apollo.

Just the two of you.
Just the two of us, yeah. We were there -- we done a week there, she and I. They sent for us.
You were here and they booked you from here.

That's right, but the greatest deal was when we played for the president, and that was -- oh, man, that was something, boy. I thought the guys was joking. Yeah, he was here for about -- I think he stayed a week or something like that. He brought all those guys with him. (Inaudible). So they

That's great.
Yeah, man, and when we --

We stayed at the Statler.
The Statler, right.
Statler Hotel.
In fact I stayed there about six weeks ago.
Is that right?
It's still there.

Nice place, isn't it? So a cab met us, you know, and taken us out there, you understand what I mean? And we open the door and in my room there were a fifth of Kentucky Tavern with a letter on it, you know, saying compliments from the president, compliments from the president.
That's great, I hope you saved that letter.
Oh, that letter's at home. Yeah, and in Julia's room the same thing.
Great. The president knew it should be bourbon and not scotch, huh?
That's right, yeah.

Two drummers. Too bad one of us didn't play another instrument, because we would have been together for the last 12 years, and we both know that.
That's right.
But unfortunately we both play drums.
Yes.

That's wonderful. right.
And as I say, I hope we both get a gig pretty soon, and I'm sure we will. Neither one of us is unemployed very long.

And now ladies and gentlemen this is Tape Two of an interview with Samuel Baby Lovett by Art Smith at the Afterhours, with very able assistance from Charles Crook Goodwin. Now to go into the interview here at the Afterhours. We were talking about some of the old rooms in Kansas City that Baby played and that Crook played and we came along with one; I thought I'd heard about most of them with my band, traveling with my band, they talked about the rooms and the people so much, but here is one called the Yellow Front, which is around 18th and Forest, where the bands used to play and it was a great place for jam sessions. Oh yes, we would start playing around eight o'clock and we'd play until five o'clock in the morning and everybody was jumping, having a good time and that was one of the greatest times of my life in the music business, playing at the Yellow Front, and they had a lady bouncer by the name of --
You talked about that in another room, the Babylon Club. Not down there, she wasn't down there. You talked about that last week.
How long did you play there, Baby? How

Well I think about a couple of years. It wasn't very long, about two years.
The cats used to come in and jam there?
Oh yeah, yeah we had a ball.
Remember who was on the band with you there? Was "Booster" there, your pal from Louisiana?
Yes, Booster was on trumpet.
What was Booster's full name?
Robert Thomas.
Robert Thomas?
That's right.
He came up from Louisiana with you --
Right.
-- and he played with you all the time -- well for a long time before he left town?
That is right, uh-huh, and Emile Williams played piano.
Oh, I've heard of him.
Oh yeah, he was a wonderful piano player. Everybody was crazy about him and we had a bouncer there called Eva Tangway.
Crook, I'm sure you've had memories of the Yellow Front. Would you tell us something about it, what you were doing there?

What I remember about the Yellow Front was the gentleman that run the Yellow Front, Ellis Burton. He was a friend to the musicians, a very good friend. If you would go by Ellis Burton and you were kind of low on cash, the musicians that he liked so well, he would always replenish them.
Was he white or black, Crook?

He was a black man and he understood operating a nightclub and he ruled with an iron hand. Whenever he would speak, I don't care what would be going on in the club, well they would cool down if Ellis would come around. He would run the joint. He kept law and order, but above all, he was a great guy and he would -- he would feed the musicians; he would cook up a big pot of spaghetti or just what have you, you know, --
Gumbo?
-- some kind of stew or gumbo or just anything and just invite us, the guys who were playing casual in town on engagements, well invite a big bunch of them down and --
After you'd finished --

-- after we finished hours, we'd all have a big feast. He's set a big, long table and boy, we would go at it. You know, all you want to drink, all you want to eat. He would do this several times a year.
Well, did you play then too, after hours down there?
Oh yeah, every night practically we'd all go by as a sort of a tribute to him. We would jam in the joint, you know, until the wee hours of the morning whenever we had a chance to do it, you know.
I would guess then you jammed with Baby's band down there?

Of course. We jammed a lot when Baby and I were playing together in a big band; Thoman Hayes' band and also the band that changed to be the Kansas City Rockets, Harlan headed by Leonard. We would go down there and we'd still go there and jam; the same consequences.
You and Baby left Thoman Hayes to go with Harlan Leonard's Rockets, Harlan Leonard's band?

Well, the band was originally Thoman's band. Thoman had a little union trouble and Harlan was voted to front the band and from then on, well Harlan did have the band. After trips to Chicago and around and down in the southern part of the country, at this time Harlan was the head of the band.

You know RCA about three years ago reissued on an LP the great Harlan Leonard band. Ernie Williams, for example, did about three vocals. Let's see, who was on that band? I know the Walter Brothers were, weren't
they or were they not?
No.
Neither one?

None of the originals that were with him before. See, possibly getting a little ahead of my story, Harlan Leonard's band also -- the Kansas City Rockets also broke up in 1936, after our second unsuccessful trip to Chicago to try to make it big and I guess most of the guys figured, "Well, this is enough. We want to play music but we will also dedicate ourselves to making a living and getting the best out of it", and then we all branched off into smaller groups.

I started playing with Buster Smith at a place called Lucille's Paradise and Baby Lovett, Herman Walder, Jack Johnson, a little place there and Pete Johnson, the great Pete Walder Johnson, the boogie woogie piano player, and the brothers, Herman and Woodie, and I believe there were six members in that band, I think I named all six of them. Well they went to play at 12th and Truce at a place called the Spinning Wheel, and this was part of the band that was a part of Leonard's band; that is, the Kansas City Rockets, and then there was another part of the band -- it's a little vague to me now, let me see, I'm trying to think of who was left, right now it escapes me -- but this is part of the way the band went in separate ways.

Well, we'll come back to the Spinning Wheel when we get into the rooms that were in town that we're going to cover. That's very interesting, Crook's description of what happened to the Harlem Leonard great band. We'll be right back ladies and gentlemen.
(Whereupon a brief recess was taken.)

From the Spinning Wheel, what do you remember of the Reno Club, Baby, because we know that -- watch your fingers on the mike. (Yeah, just like that. There you go, right. An old drummer, you should be able to hold a mike, huh. I know that you know that Basie played there but do you have anything to tell us about it?

Well, I was working at the Spinning Wheel at 12th and Truce and the Reno Nightclub I guess was about a couple of blocks down on the same side of the street and when we'd have intermission, I would go down and see Basie, talk to him until my time was up, you understand what I mean, and then when they'd have intermission, he'd come by the Spinning Wheel and talk to me, see.

So we did that the whole time I was at the Spinning Wheel and I was there a pretty good while. I guess I was there about -- at least two or three years, two years at the Spinning Wheel and that was during the good old days. We'd go to work at eight o'clock, get off at five in the morning and we were getting paid back in those days, your highest salary
for the hours, I was getting $2.50 a night, playing from eight until five in the morning.
That's a side man. What did the leader get?
Three, $3.00. So I did that for a long time at the Spinning Wheel there and when I left the Spinning Wheel --
Well now, you're talking about the Spinning Wheel when you were there. Was that your band because Crook just got finished talking about being there with part of Harlan Leonard's great, famous band?
That was my band at the Spinning Wheel.
You mean you had the- Harlan Leonard group, that was your band that Crook was talking about? Right, great, wonderful.

And we would get off -- I said -- I mentioned this, that we'd get off about five o'clock in the morning, you know, but as long as there was someone there we'd play, you see, and our highest deal, the leader, was $2.50.
The tips were good though?
Oh yeah. Sometimes we didn't need the salary, man, we got all tips, you know what I mean.
What did you do at five o'clock when you finished?
Go home.
You went home. What did you do Crook?
Well, sometimes we'd go home. For the most part if we found anybody at 12th and Woodland, this was the Sunset Club --
Next on the list.
-- and this was where --

It would appear that we're going into the next club here, the Sunset Club. I think that's great because it's a famous room of the '30s, the great Kansas City jazz days, and Crook just led into that naturally. Tell us about the Sunset Club.

Well this was a place that operated without a key to the front door. There was no key. You could ask Piney Brown, say, 'Piney, where's the key'? 'We never did have a key. I didn't have one made when I opened the place'. So this is the way he would operate it. Any big band that come through here, well their musicians would end up at the Sunset for the big jam session.
Sometimes the band would be 10 and 12 pieces. They only hired Pete Johnson and Merl Johnson, which have no relation.
The great drummer Merl Johnson, a fabulous guy with the rim shots. I remember him so well.
Yes. They played there for years but the band would always be augmented to 10 or 12. I can recall
back guys like Louie Armstrong and Jack Teagarden, just to name a couple of the great musicians.
Cliffey Leeman told me he sat in there one time and Gene Krupa told me he sat in there one time.

Any musician that come through Kansas City during the late '20s and the early '30s, if he hadn't played and jammed at the Sunset, well he really hadn't been to Kansas City. It was just that simple. He had to come to the Sunset because that's where it was happening.
Marty Napoleon said the same thing. When he came through it was Chico Marx's band, played the mule box.
All guys that come through here I don't care how great they were, they would be at the Sunset.

Now you mentioned Piney Brown and I'd like to ask both of you what you have memories of Piney Brown. You know, to an Easterner years and years ago reading and listening to Kansas City jazz and reading about it, Piney Brown was almost a mythical character. He was almost beyond belief and then when I came here to Kansas City, I found that he was very much alive, very much a real figure and the Piney Brown blues that's written and played today, still today, is a fairly true picture of Piney Brown. Who would like to talk first about Piney Brown? Baby.
Oh you want -- Crook.
Crook, all right.

Well, you would remember Piney Brown. You'd have to remember him for the big time spender. Whenever -- well say the party would be of a size of 10 or 12 people. Well there was nobody spending any money but Piney Brown. He didn't want anybody to spend any money. He was the big spender at any club. He would take -- sometime he would leave with a bunch of musicians and people from his club, and this was a time when segregation was at its highest --
What year would that be or years?
That would be, oh, along about '29 and '31. Piney would take a bunch of people to most any white place in town --
Black people.

-- and black people couldn't go in there but Piney could. He was your entry, he'd get you in there and they would set a big table for him because Piney was going to spend more money than the rest of the people all put together and they had to almost let him in. They wanted his money. This revenue kept him going. It was --
So they forgot segregation?
That's right, they forgot what color it was and he had some free money.
That was the equalizer. Crook, tell me, where did Piney get his money? I think most of us might know
but we'd like to hear it from a native Kansas Citian who played the music.

Piney was -- actually Piney operated the policy wheel. He had -- he made plenty of money. In fact, if I'm not mistaken, I think he had two or three policy wheels in town. Him and another fellow -- this was a white fellow by the name of Bud Smith I believe it was -- they both operated the bigtime policy wheel thing in town and this was -- this was where Piney got money and it was another fellow here by the name of Felix Payne who also backed Piney in his policy venture.

Felix Payne was a top -- one of the top gamblers in town and there was another fellow by the name of Little Piney. There was a Big Piney and a Little Piney. They both were gamblers and but when Big Piney was the last of the bigtime spenders. He would -- Piney would always furnish the money.
Well, let me ask this Crook. When they talk about Piney Brown, I would guess they were talking about Big Piney?
Big Piney.
Big Piney always, and who wrote 'Piney Brown Blues'?
I can't remember. I don't know whether it was --
Joe Turner did something.
Joe Turner did the vocals on it --
Right.
-- because Joe Turner --
It was Big Johnson on piano.
Right, because they were -- they had worked for -- see Joe worked for Piney.
At the Sunset?
At the Sunset. Joe was a singer but I hadn't mentioned this before but he was a singer.
Joe Turner?
Yes.
Big Joe. Well, we'll get on to him. We'll get on to him in the interview.
Pete Johnson was the piano player and Merl Johnson was the drummer.
Merl Johnson, so fabulous with rim shots, yes. May God rest his soul.
And they -- well at this time, as I said, Piney would furnish the money for all the parties and everything.
At the Sunset?

At the Sunset or wherever. If you'd meet him on the street, well he was a guy that, 'Come on, let's have a drink' or what have you. 'You hungry, need something to eat' or just anything. Just a way to spend money. He was
just that much of a spender.
He took good care of his musicians.
Right.
Paid probably more than other owners in town?
No.
He paid the same scale?
This was the same thing --
Except he laid it off on tips?

-- except he would give you money. He'd come in a joint where you were playing when he knew you and he would stuff money in your clothes or anything, you know. "Come on and have a drink", and he was -- as I say, he was about the biggest spender in this man's town, Kansas City, Missouri.
And you liked him, not only for the money but I mean --
Everybody. You had to like him.
You trusted him and you liked him?
Right, right. He never would do anything, you know, where it would hurt you. I just -- with some of the others, he was a man that loved life and lived life.
How did he die? Did he die a natural death?
Yes, he did.
Here in Kansas City?
No. He went to open up a big policy thing on the West Coast but this venture never did happen because soon he fell ill and he died out on the West Coast.
I see. Baby, what do you remember of Baby -- of Piney Brown I mean, excuse me?

I don't think there's very much left to say about Piney because Crook has mentioned everything I know about Piney but everything is true what Crook was telling you about Piney. Everybody loved him. Everybody, and money didn't mean nothing to Piney.
If a bunch of people were sitting in a joint somewhere and wasn't nothing on the table, Piney would fill the table up for them; just everybody. He was just one of those type of guys.
Black and white?
Yeah, yeah, everybody.
But you know Crook mentioned Little Piney Brown. Now was there any relationship between Little Piney Brown and the Piney Brown?

Now this -- I heard that they were brothers. Now this I don't know; but I always know that Piney treated him as a younger brother. Little Piney was younger. They called him Little Piney because he was younger but he
was a larger man than Big Piney but they called him Little Piney because of his age and I just imagined that they were kin.
Was he in the policy racket too?

I don't know what he did for a living. I know he played a lot of golf. He played a lot of golf. You know, every time I'd see him, most any day, you know, early day or the afternoon he'd have on golf togs and this is all I've ever seen him do.
Well, what ever happened to Little Piney?
The last time that I heard of Little Piney it was in the '40s. I think he passed before Big Piney. He lived in Chicago.
In Chicago?
He had moved away from Kansas City to Chicago and I saw him once in Chicago in the late '30s but after that I think he passed in the early '40s just before Big Piney.
And Big Piney was buried on the West Coast, was he?
I don't remember.
He made such a name for himself here, I just wondered about it.
I don't think they brought the body
back here. I think he was buried on the West Coast.
Now Baby, you played at Piney Brown's Sunset Cafe, right?
Yeah.
And that was the Harlan Leonard band, part of the Leonard band then?
Well just -- I think the bass man was from Leonard and that's about all I know from Harlan's band.
Who else was on that band, do you remember?
Well now I remember -- the names of those guys, man it's kind of tough for me now.
Well tell me, when did you play with Bunk Johnson here in Kansas City?
Oh, that was way back -- way back, I guess about in the '30s.
Well, it's all way back.
Yeah, pretty far back and as I once said, we played at the Yellow Front.
That's right. Bunk Johnson played with you at the Yellow Front?
That's right.
Now you never played with Bunk down in New Orleans and down in Louisiana?
No.
Bunk played with you here in Kansas City?
That is right.

Now how did that New Orleans horn fit into your Kansas City jazz up here, because you played New Orleans drums I know, Louisiana drums. All you Louisiana drummers have that fabulous roll. I always catch that every-time from a Louisiana drummer but did Bunk fit in with the rest of the guys all right?
Oh yes, he played Dixie. We were playing Dixieland blues.
You were playing Dixie up here?
Yeah. You know, that's all Bunk knew from New Orleans. You know, he was born in New Orleans --
Oh yeah.
-- and --
Where was Kid Ory in those days, was he back in New Orleans?
Yeah, he was in New Orleans, yeah and--
George Lewis I guess he was down -- he didn't leave New Orleans until the '50s did he?
No, no.
Wouldn't go out on the road, never?
Couldn't get him away from there.
Couldn't get him away from there.
Had a hard time getting me from down in there, man. You know, down in Alexandria, Louisiana. It's hard to get those guys to stay up here, you know what I mean.
Well, I notice they all seem to go back.
Oh yeah.
Georgie Brunies went back, Freddie Kohlman went back, they all seem to migrate back home again, you know, back to New Orleans.

That's right. They'll go back there all right because that's home to those guys, you know, and the first thing the guys ask when they come up here, "Say man, you know where I can get some red beans and rice".
Yeah, that's right.
I say sure you can get red beans and rice and I take them to the Chinese joints, you understand, and let them eat all the red beans and rice they want.

Well Baby, red beans and rice. Freddie Kohlman was up here, as Crook knows, and man he cooked us red beans and rice every Sunday while he was booked way downtown with the Dukes of Dixieland, but anyway, I want to finish this side one of Tape No. 2 and we will carry on and we can carry on with Bunk Johnson and many of the other famous and great musicians that made jazz history along with the rooms in which this music was played.

Now I've got a list of these rooms, I've got a list of these musicians and I'll really ask both of you to interject a name at anytime where I don't have it so this is the end of Side One of Tape Two at the Afterhours with the interview of Baby Lovett, the great Samuel Baby Lovett, with Crook Goodwin and yours truly, Art Smith. We'll be right back with Side Two of Tape Two.
(End of Side One, Tape Two.)

Side Two of Tape Two of the interview with Samuel Baby Lovett, the nationally known and famous Kansas City jazz drummer, with Crook Goodwin, the great guitarist and vocalist, who's helped himself to make so much of Kansas City jazz history, who is currently with Art Smith's Kansas City Jazz Band. This is yours truly, Art Smith.

We were talking about Bunk Johnson. I think the interesting thing was that Baby and Bunk played together here in Kansas City rather than down in New Orleans. Now I think I would like to get on to one of the really truly famous, best known, Kansas City jazz musicians -- people might think of Count Basie when I say that but really I'm talking about Benny Moten, Benny Moten "Moten" Swing, and there's so much to tell about him.
I think there are things that can be told on this tape that are not in books that I learned when I came out here in 1962, organized my band and traveled with my band. I

personally used to buy Benny Moten records when I was 14, 15 years of age, the old 78s. Booker T. Washington was featured on trumpet with that band and he's now with the Art Smith Kansas City Jazz Band. I would have bet you a million to one against that ever happening when I was a boy back home in Boston, but now I'd like to talk about Benny Moten.

I'd like somebody to tell us about when the band was in Denver and when Benny came back, had that tonsillectomy done by the surgeon here and what happened but anyway, let's start out with Benny Moten; what kind of a man he was, what kind of a band leader and musician and what your personal feelings were about the great Benny Moten. Baby, did you ever play for Benny Moten?
Oh, I've sit in his band. I've sit in. I never played with him. I never played with Benny Moten's band. I was with George Lee's band during the time Benny was famous around here.
Well you must have known him?
Oh yes, I knew Benny well, I know him well. We used to play pool together.
Was he a good pool player?
Pretty good. He'd beat me, that's one thing and so he was a wonderful man, wonderful man and that night I was on 18th Street when he and Dr. Bruce, they were running together, you know.
Dr. Bruce was the surgeon that operated on Benny?
That's right.
They were pals?
That's right, and they went out and had been drinking that night and I remember that out on 18th Street that night.
What night was that, the night before the operation?
Yes, that was before the operation, yeah.
The night before?

The night before, yeah, and we were having a good time and playing pool and all that kind of stuff together so they went out that night and Dr. Bruce -- and Benny's throat was bothering him some kind of way I understand. I don't know what it was and so they both had been drinking and he went and had the operation that same night.
The next day you mean.
The next day I mean, the next day. He had the operation and that was it.
About this operation, I do believe that if Dr. Bruce had had any inkling that there was something like this going to happen, I don't think he would have even --

I think he would have turned it over to somebody else to perform the tonsillectomy because he loved Benny and Dr. Bruce was a fine physician, he was a fine man. He did like musicians and this is the last thing in the world that he would have wanted to happen to Benny Mother but I guess it was just -- I guess this could have happened if he hadn't been out the night before. It's just one of those things that happened.

Well, as I understand it, the band was in Denver and Bill Saunders, the great tenor saxophone player, with whom we've all played at one time or another or who has played with us, brought Benny back to town for that operation.
Right.
What you're saying is that when Bill and Benny got to town, Benny and Dr. Bruce went out on the town that night --
Not too much out on the town but Dr. Bruce was a person who loved nightclubs. He was in nightclubs every night and he loved Benny but really I think my first time --

Well, what happened? As I understand it, a vein was cut during the operation, because a tonsillectomy is a fairly simple operation, and a vein or an artery was cut and Benny died on the operating table at the age of 35 --
Right.
-- which would indicate a mistake was made on the part of the surgeon.
Right.
The books say that he died of a heart attack on the table but all you Kansas City jazz musicians say that's not so. What you say is that a mistake was made on the operating table.

It was an accident, a slip of the scalpel. That's the only way I can term it. Now this was -- I wasn't there in the hospital when it happened but this is the version of what most people had said and during the time that it happened. Well, I remember that Dr. Bruce was very low about the whole thing, you know, and it just seemed like it took everything out of him.
He didn't stay in Kansas City much longer. He went to Washington, D. C.

Well, that is the -- I would think the true story of what happened to the great, the only Benny Moten. That's sort of the end of his story but I would like to carry on with Benny through the years when he was alive and playing here and giving work to so many people, including William Count Basie.
Can you tell me about some of the rooms that he played in, Baby and Crook? Who was with him, when was Moten
Swing written and who wrote it and you might also tell us about Bus Moten just after this quick break if you will hold on please.
(Whereupon, a brief recess was taken.)

Now Baby knew Benny very well as every one did in those days but Crook Goodwin was a definite colleague of his and they came up together and Crook probably can give information from the one and the only Benny Moten that has never been seen in print before and I think will be of interest to the world and to the future generations. Crook.
Art, I might go back to the time -- I think at this time I'll inject Bus Moten.
Who was- Bus?
Bus was Benny's nephew. His name was not Bus Molton. His name was Iris Smith. He was Benny's sister's child. Everybody thought that Benny was Bus's father but actually he was his uncle.
Many people thought they were brothers too, you know.

Yeah, but this was what their kinship was. He was Bus's uncle but they were very close. I remember Bus when we were young kids going along and I would follow Bus all over town because Bus was one of the few guys in the gang who could walk on his hands. He was great and adept at anything he would do. He could -- he was a good

tap dancer, a beautiful tap dancer. He could have made his living that way. He played piano, which he played beautifully, which when he died he was still doing a single on piano. He played, of course, with Benny's band but before I got into that part of it, I would like to go back to the time when I knew Benny when I was a kid.

Benny wasn't much more than a kid himself and he was playing in these -- well, these houses of ill-repute, these whorehouses and so forth, and he was doing this by himself. Well he did this -- well he was -- actually I don't think Benny was of age when he was doing this but he was such an accomplished piano player that he would do this for a living. He made pretty good money at it.

All right, it comes along when he got good enough so that people thought, 'Why don't you get a couple of musicians or like a drummer and a singer and go and do dances for us'. Now there was a hall at that time called the Lyric Hall. It was a small place on 18th and Lydia, and this is where the black population mostly gave most of their dances. It would hold about 300 people, 350, and this is where they wanted Benny.

Well Benny got so he'd play there about three times a week. Now the name of the band was BB&D, Benny, Bailey and Duke I can't think of this Bailey fellow's first name but all of them -- Duke Knox -- I mean Duke Langford, sorry, was
Dude a drummer and was a very accomplished drummer.
Excuse me, Crook, about what year would this be?

This would be about 1922, and Benny was a great piano player as I said before, and this Bailey was a singer. He was a stand-up singer and he was one of the people, you know, what we call the old "shouters" and they made it big.
Well at this time George Lee had a band but he had a small band. He had a larger band than Benny at that time. I think he had about a six piece band. Benny only had three.
Was Baby on that George Lee band?

No, not at that time. The band had augmented when Baby got with the band and they had a 12 piece band. Before that time Benny augmented his band slowly. I think he made almost a jump from the three pieces to about 11 or 12 pieces. He had a guy that I admired very much. We called him Banjo Joe. This is a time when banjos were very popular and he was one of the greatest around then. He had a style of picking a banjo that, you know, was unique at that time. Nobody else did it like him and you could go back to Okeh Records where Benny cut Okeh Records, you know, before and up to I think it was Victor Records he went to and made records and you'll hear this guy, Banjo Joe. He was one of the stalwarts with Benny's band but he was -- maybe he would

be on the gig and maybe he wouldn't.
I've seen the time when he would be on his way to the gig and there was a place where the lady made this Oklahoma chalk. It was about three or four doors from me and this woman would call him in to give him a drink of chalk and he --
What was chalk?

Well chalk is an Oklahoma drink; I don't know, it's made from some grain. It's a thing something like beer but you can drink it hot. It doesn't have to be cold. It can be hot, you know, but it will knock you for a loop, and Banjo Joe would stop in there and get a couple of drinks and then he'd pull his banjo out and start working there at this little place and everybody -- this would help the woman bring in business for the chalk joint and Benny would be without a banjo player, but this went along for a little while and Benny finally had to let Joe go.
All during this time Benny was building up a big reputation as a band leader.
In Kansas City.
In Kansas City.
Who were some of the other people joining the band, Crook, at that time?
Jack Washington.
Oh, the great Jack Washington, yes.
Now he went with Basie --
Played alto and baritone.
Well, didn't he go with Basie?
He went with Basie. Harlan Leonard.
Oh the great Harlan Leonard.
Woody Walder, tenor man.
Herman's brother.
Herman Walder's brother, and let me see -- Walter Page.
On bass.
On bass.
Was that before the Blue Devils?
Not on the bass -- I'm ahead of myself. Vernon Keys was the bass player.
Vernon Keys was the bass player, and Mack Washington was on drums?
Mack Washington was on drums. Mack Washington was before any of the rest of them because I think he was with Benny when Benny had about six pieces. He was a kind of flashy drummer.
Now this was before the Harlan Leonard band?
Right.
And the Thoman Hayes band?
Right.
Right, all before that.
Yes. Now, as I can remember it, Benny began to just grab up most of the work in Kansas City, you know, most of the big band work. At this time --
Steady gigs, casual dates?
Steady gigs and what have you. He went on the best jobs.
Did he pay well?
Yes.
For the time, for the period?
Yes.
He was a good man to work for?
Yeah. He made good money and he was good to his men.
He paid over scale?
Yeah. Well, scale as we knew it then. It didn't have to be very much to be over scale because I think the scale at the tops was about $6.00 a night.
Well, as he went along, he was playing the various rooms, the good rooms in town on casual dates and adding to his band, he must have been very well established when Basie came to town?
Oh yeah, he definitely was.
When was that?
Basie came to Kansas City about --
I've got to think about this -- it was about 1927.
Wasn't he with a traveling show?
It was Gonzelle White's show.
Gonzelle White. They --
They played here at the Gayiety Theatre and they became stranded -- they ran out of money. I guess the money that they made at the Gayiety didn't help them too much because they broke up here.
Well when the band broke up, what did Basie do first -- the very first thing he did? Was he playing around town, looking for gigs?

Right. The first time I was working at a place called the Bluebird at 18th and Grove. It was an upstairs joint and this was during Prohibition and, you know, they sold a little hard stuff on the side, you know, to make it, and we had a piano player there by the name of Dude Knox. I think Baby remembers Dude. Dude
Dude Knox, I believe the same one you were talking about earlier. No, Dude Lanford you were talking about earlier, right, right.

And there were about five of us playing in this place and we saw a guy come along, he looked like anything but a musician and oh boy, we were playing away you know and this guy -- I didn't know who he was and he came and stood right by the piano and looked, he kept looking

down at the piano and Dude would look up at him. Neither one of them said anything and finally between numbers Basie looked at Dude and said, "Man, you ain't playing nothing". He said, "Why don't you get on up" and Dude politely gave him the seat, which when Basie started to playing, boy the house just turned around. You know, he just shocked everybody in the house.
He was an accomplished piano player.
Well, he was an accomplished piano player as such with his style.
Was that the Kansas City style?
Not really. This was more like --
I was told that Sleepy Hickocks, had a great deal to do with Basie's style.
After he was around here for a while.
That's true?
The man who was responsible more or less, if you listen to Fats Waller, Fats Waller taught Basie organ.
Personally or from the record.
Personally.
Personally. Back in New York?
See, they knew each other out East.
See most people think Basie is from Kansas City but Basie is from Bank, New Jersey. He knew Fats Waller and if you listen to Fats Waller's records and listen to Basie, you can
see that Basie was sort of orientated by Fats Waller
But he was really influenced though by Kansas City pianists I understand?

Well after he got here he didn't want to leave because he could gather up a whole lot of -- there was a lot of things going on. There was a little guy where -- we had mentioned a place called the Yellow Front. There was a little guy down there, young fellow, very young, Jimmy Jones, which God rest his soul, he didn't live very long, but that little guy was one of the greatest piano players.
Was he playing at a joint downtown?
He was playing at the Yellow Front.
At the Yellow Front, right.
At the Yellow Front.
Boy, that must have been quite a place.
Oh it was. See all the musicians --
Well anyway Basie came along and played gigs. Did he ever front his own band in those days before he went with Moten or was he playing as a sideman?
No, he played more or less as a side man.
Did he do singles too?
Yes. All of us would do little gigs, you know, whichever one got the job.
Like it is today.

Or you'd be the leader. It's just the same. Nothing's changed but at this time well Basie was scrambling around and playing here and playing there but he liked Benny's band because Benny had a well established band and had a great band, one of the greatest in Kansas City if not the greatest, and he, at this time it was George Lee and Benny Moten Melton.
Well these two bands were the biggest and the best bands in Kansas City.
And George Lee was the band Baby, you were with?
Yes.
Well during this time up until about 19 -- I think that Baby went with George about 1928, I think it was.
It was in the '20s I know.
It was '27 or '28, around there.
Well tell us how Basie went with Moten Melton?

Oh, this is a story. Basie had a -- well first of all, Baby had a -- Benny had a -- he used Basie off and on, you know. Basie liked the band so well he would hang around and he didn't want any money. He just wanted the pleasure of playing with Benny.
He would sit in for Benny Moten Melton?
He would sit in for Benny.
Benny Moten would get off the piano stool and Basie would sit down and play?
Right.
This would be on a gig, right on a gig?
Yeah, right on a job.
In a saloon downtown?
Yeah. Well on a club date or something like that, a casual.
In other words, Basie sat in for Moten when Moten would let him?
He just loved the band that much and Benny got a job --
Well Booker, I guess was on the band then?
Oh yeah.
Well, we'll get to Booker later. Go ahead.
Benny got a job in Wichita, Kansas, in a ballroom down there, I forget the name of the ballroom, but anyway he had a job there. It was a steady engagement, steady work six nights a week.
For a period of weeks?
Yeah. I guess he was going to be down there six weeks or eight weeks or something like that, and all the guys met -- Benny, he and Thamon Hayes ran a record
shop on 18th Street and this is where the guys would assemble when they would go out of town. You know, the bus there would pick them up or even if they were going on --
You mean Thomas Hayes' band and Moten's band?
No, Moten's band. This existed when the record shop was operating. Thomas and Benny run this record shop.
Right.

They sold records, you know, and the guys would be down in there whenever they were going out of town so they'd have one central meeting place, right, and they'd meet at this place to leave town. Well this particular night when they was ready to go to Wichita --
Benny Moten's band?
Benny Moten's band, Basie comes along.
And they met in this record shop that was owned by Benny and Thomas.
Right. They'd come along -- Basie come along and he was all packed, had his roll or whatever it was --
All his belongings?
Yeah, he had everything and Benny come up and asked him, 'Where you going'? He said, 'I'm going

with you fellows". He said, "Well, I don't need a piano player, I'm a piano player myself", and you know, it's one of these things that sounds more like a kid is saying, you know, "Well, I won't be any trouble". "Well, I can't pay you anything". "That's all right, I'll go anyway".

Well, the guys got together and said, "Well, why not, let him go". "Okay, we'll knock a dollar or a dollar or two off my salary to give it to him, you know, so he can get along". Well, they liked Basie this much, you know. Actually Benny liked him.
He must have had a nice personality?
Oh, he did. He had an infectious personality.
Infectious, right.
You know, he could just worm his way in to anything. So this is the way he started with Benny's band, Now when Benny left Wichita and he came back to Kansas City --
Did Bill Saunders come back with him?
Bill Saunders wasn't with the band.
He wasn't with the band?
Not then.
Benny came back to Kansas City by himself?
No, he came back with the band.
With the band?

They finished the engagement in Wichita. They had commitments in Fairlawn Park in Kansas City, which was about the best job in town. This was about the best paying job or big paying. You played there nightly, seven nights a week. I think the salary for a sideman, and I worked there about three different times, I think the salary for a sideman was $57.00 per week, and this was the biggest money.
Yeah, that's where Andy Kirk got his start.

They wouldn't let him sit in. Why not?

Yeah, and they would laugh at him, wouldn't let him sit in.

Well, he had a family here, his mother and father. At least a mother...
Oh, the family was right down the street from me.
Oh, he lived with his mother?
Yeah, it was about a block and a half, 16th Street. Yeah, but Charlie never run with anybody. I never seen him with anybody, always by himself, walking with his head down.
I guess he was pretty young in those days. He was only about 35 when he died.
Yeah, he was a young guy. The guys wouldn't let him sit in. He was too far.
He was too good for them, is that what you're saying?

No.

-- he'd always come to Ernie Williams or myself and he would try to get information. 'You fellows have been around, you've been in the game. What must I do here?', and you know, he wanted information about life, not music.
