He would eat because it's necessary to eat to keep alive, and I've heard he made this expression after he got famous.

The only thing he cared about a place to eat and rest and play his horn. Now these are the three basic things that Charlie Parker liked, that he cared about. I mean, any other thing in the world -- say, most guys go for big automobiles when they make some money; well, Charlie didn't. I don't think he ever --
Well, what was he like when you went and had a drink with him somewhere on intermission or after a gig was over?

He was a swell young guy. But Charlie never did give himself time to let himself out with people and be with people and he was a warm person but, I don't know, there was something that he'd always manage to be moving. He

was just -- oh I might say just too far ahead of his time. He just pushed himself into everything, you know. He reminded me more or less of say like a candlefly flying around the light. Let's go, let's go. Everything is moving and we've got to go and, you know, he was just full of life, wanted to go and just going all the time and he didn't have too much time for people as such, you know. I mean he just wanted to --
Excuse me, Crook. Baby, how did you find him personally to have a drink with or have lunch with or whatever?

Well, I never drank with him. I never had a drink with Charlie. I don't know how he acted after he got a drink in him. I don't know but he was an awful nice guy when I saw him all the time. He wasn't drunk, I'll tell you that much. He wasn't drunk.
Well, just one second, I have to change something here. We'll be right back.
(Whereupon, a brief recess was taken.)
Now, I'd like to ask you, Baby, and you Crook about the Charlie Parker Foundation, what it is set up to do and what you think the future will be. What do you think, Baby?
I think it will be a great thing.
What is it?
It's something -- it's supposed to be a statue, isn't it?
Well, it's a foundation.
Yeah, but they're supposed to build a statue.
Crook, you answer now.
Yeah, the Charlie Parker Foundation is a thing to glorify Charlie Parker.
Not Kansas City jazz?
Well --
Or Only incidentally.
Kansas City jazz would be secondary. This is strictly for Charlie Parker. It's the Charlie Parker Foundation.
Memorial.

Yes, but it's more or less a thing for young people. They have set up a standard where they teach young kids to play instruments. They have teachers that are hired and I think they have a government grant to operate it.
Now, they also have built -- have built a number of homes in these, you know, these two dwelling homes or whatever they call them, they're like duplexes. They're up --
Low income housing?
Yeah, low income housing. They instituted this through government funds and through raising money and they had a big thing here some years back where

Ella Fitzgerald, Mary Lou Williams and quite a few of the greats were here and at this particular housing project they have streets named after Mary Lou Williams, Ella Fitzgerald and several of the big names that did come and offer their services.
Yeah, Basie came in for that too, I believe?

Basie. See they named these streets in this project after these people and it's a wonderful thing, I can say, but I don't know too much about the financial part of the Charlie Parker Foundation at present because I don't know how long their grant from the government will last and I don't know -- I heard the other day that they are moving. I think they're moving out to Multipurpose Center out on Linwood, and I do hope that they continue.

Well, you know, it seems to me, gentlemen, that so many other Kansas City musicians did so much more for Kansas City music than Charlie Parker did and I can see a foundation for Kansas City jazz as such and with the names of all the great people that are still with us and so many that have passed being immortalized in a foundation. That's just my viewpoint. What do you think of that, Crook?
Well, I do think -- I think you have a great point there. I think in these terms. There are so many great musicians that come up around Kansas City as did
Charlie Parker and Ben Webster. Ben Webster was born --
Oh, we can go on and on and on.
We can go on and on naming quite a few musicians.
I was thinking about the next person Jay McShann, I want to talk about, W McSham for example.

Well Jis out of Muskogee, Oklahoma. He came here at a very young age. I was playing with Jay I guess back in the early '30s when Jay was playing -- we both were playing small nightclubs and we got together and we played at a place called Wolf's Tavern.
Who was the leader of the band?
Jay
Jay and you were his guitar player and vocalist. Wolf's Tavern, right downtown.
18th and Vine Streets and we played there for a while and I did quite a bit of work like that. I worked with Emil Williams like that, playing guitar and vocal.

Well, I never knew Emil but Jis a dear friend of mine and just a beautiful guy and it seems to me the numbers that he's written and the music he's played, that's Kansas City Jazz. He's not the only one to personify it but surely he's one of the leading exponents of it, whereas I can never consider Charlie Parker a leading exponent of
Kansas City jazz.
Well, he got some experience from Jay McShann.
Well, he worked for Jay too, didn't he, right.
He went to New York with Jay McShann's band in New York in 1941?
Oh, what happened to Jay McShann's band in New York in 1941?

They had -- Al Hibler, you know, was with Jay McShann, because I was in the service then and a fellow from New York was in my company in the service and I had told this fellow that -- he was a clarinet player -- I told him, I said, "I know Jay McShann very well", and he said, "Well who is this guy that they had to lead to the microphone to sing"?
Oh Al Hibler, yeah.
Well, I didn't know that Al Hibler was with Jay.
You didn't know Al Hibler in Kansas City?
No, I have -- I had never met him. I hadn't heard of him but what I thought, he had a singer, a blues singer with him, Walter Brown --
Oh yes.
-- and it first came to my mind that Walter Brown had gone blind.
Oh I see.
Well, I had no way of knowing. I was in the service. I'm out of connection. See, I had lost contact with the fellows.
And you thought Walter Brown had gone blind?
I thought, I said, 'Well it must have been Walter Brown' because this guy he didn't know Al Hibbler either because Al Hibbler was famous then.
Basie, of course, did a lot for Al Hibbler.
Basie and the Duke.
And the Duke, yeah.
See, he sang with the Duke, but he was a beautiful.
But Jay keeps going on and on with that Territory Band making albums. He just made one in New York not too long ago and he was at the party Sunday night. Did you see him there?
Right, right.
He and his lovely wife, Maryann. Baby, what do you know about Jay? You must know a lot about him. Did you ever play for Jay?
No, never played for Jay. He always -- he wanted me, though, (inaudible). He'd tell me, he'd say, 'If anything ever
Who was he using, Gus Johnson in those days, I guess?
Yeah, Gus, and he's told me that since Paul has been working with him.
Oh, Paul Gunter?
Yeah, he tells me that right now.
Well, you're a fabulous drummer, everybody know that, Baby.
He says, 'You're my drummer'. I say, 'Well I'm ready'. I never run with Jay, you know.
Well, you know, I don't think you ran with many people, Baby. Really, I think you went home every night afterwards.
I did.
You went home to Tillie.
That's right. I didn't do much running, not very much running. Still, I don't do much running.
No, but you seem to show up at the right places like Sunday night I was so happy to see you at that big party, the musicians union party.
I don't miss things like that.
Les Brown did a nice job.
Oh man, that's a band.
Same old band.
It sure is. ^ Butch Stone, Stumpy.
I liked that drummer, boy.
Oh, that's Jack Sperling.
He was something wasn't he?
He's fantastic, bad man.
What --
Well, he did all that wonderful stuff + 'Londonderry Air,' 'Blue Lou.' with Pete Fountain, 'Londonderry Air,' 'Blue, Blue'.
First time I ever heard him.
Well here's the tribute that I myself would like to pay to Baby Lovett.
Crook Goodwin speaking now.

I played with Lovett about five years, big band, we were on the road traveling. He is one of the few drummers, you know, that I've played with, you know, he's just like a metronome. He sets a tempo --
And that's it.
-- and you can do whatever you want to do. He's going to --
Be there when you come back.
-- hold you right in tow. There won't be any -- you can run off if you want to but you'll be out there by yourself.
(Laughter)
That's a great compliment.
Thank you very much.

He wouldn't give an inch, you know. There's no way that he's going to follow you. He's going to keep that same beat but after a while I imagine the guy that would be off, when -- well he'd come back to what he was doing because he's not going to budge. See, this is what makes him a great drummer. This is what makes him the way he is.

I'm sure many people must have thought so with the following he's had over the years, which brings us up to these albums. There are so many of them I don't know where to begin. How did -- you know, what kind of -- you worked for Bobby Sherwood quite a bit on the Coast making records.
Yes.
How was he as a boss?
Oh, wonderful, wonderful, a wonderful person. He was a wonderful person to work for, I'll tell you that much; just everything smooth with him. He doesn't get excited at all and I think --
Pretty good trumpet player?
Oh man, pretty good -- in the meantime Red Nichols was on the deal.
Oh yeah, well you worked with Red Nichols, yes.
That's right.
How was Red Nichols to work with?
Oh man, it was fine. He used to like a little taste.
Well why not.
And Julia was right with him, you know.
Was Julia on piano in all these?
Yeah.
And vocals.
Yeah.
How did you get -- how did you work your drums in with the vibes of Red Norvell?
Well, I just --
You just kept it steady.
-- used brushes.
Brushes?
Yeah. When you're [fishing] a man, you don't use a whole lot of sticks.
What did you say, when you're fishing a man?
Fishing.
Fishing?
Featuring a man. You don't use the sticks, you know, especially with vibes, you know. You've got to feel with him.
Was Norvo the leader on those or was -- I know he's on quite a few of them. Was he the leader?
No.
Sherwood the leader?
Yeah, yeah.
You know, I was just looking at some Jay McShann of these W McShann here. Crook, do you want to say something?
Yes. I remember -- I don't remember how many times that Lovett and Julia went to the Coast and made records.
Three times.

Three different times and I think what I was hoping, I was hoping they would continue on away from Kansas City when they had a chance to be -- I think if they had continued on -- which was no fault of Baby Lovett's, himself, I think that they would have both ended up being millionaires. I think they were just that great because when they would go away on these -- to make records and they were playing different places, well these agents would come to them and they just had their future mapped out for them and the money was there, you know. They could practically name their price or what they wanted to travel and I think it more or less was Julia was a home girl and she just loved Kansas City and she just never did care too much about leaving and staying away from Kansas City.
Well Crook, you refer to her agent.
Uh --
Johnny.
Johnny, yeah.
Johnny Tomino, well he's still around. Well, no he just died didn't he? He's still booking.
He's still living.
Oh, he's retired, but he booked you and Julia out on the Coast?
Yeah.
Well, did he line up Norvel and your dates with Norvel and Bobby Sherwood and Red Nichols? Who lined those dates up?
I don't know.
The guy from Kansas City.
Dave Dexter.
Dave Dexter.
He lined this up while you and Julia were on the Coast?
Yeah, that's right, Dave Dexter.
Now who was he with?
Dave Dexter was --
Capitol Records.
-- Capitol Records.
Yeah, well he loved jazz, a lot of wonderful liner notes but I didn't know that he went and made bookings too -- arranged bookings.
Well, it wasn't so much the bookings. It was after --
Capitol Record dates, right. He didn't book them into the joints. He booked them into the record dates, now I've got it.
He took care of the record dates. He was responsible for the different guys and the different people that they played with while they were on the Coast.
He evidently -- from what I hear about Dave Dexter, --
(Unintelligible).
Yes, that's exactly what I've heard from everybody, that he's done more for jazz musicians. Well, he and John Hammond would be neck in neck in that respect.
Well, he stopped me from using brushes while we were recording.
Yeah, well I --
He -- (inaudible) -- "shish","shish", that's what he's hearing now, you see, and it interferes with the recording so I had to use sticks all the way.
Yeah but now you know you hear some

beautiful brush work when you hear -- like Georgie Whetling Berigan's on "I Can't Get behind Bunny Burg on the solo and it kind of got started in what, 1936, '37. I would hate to have had sticks on that, you know, to listen to, to my ear, some of the stuff Shelly Manne's done with those brushes and Krupa with that small group, you know, "The Wire Brush Stomp".
Well maybe Dave Dexter -- you know, I'm sure he knew what he was doing.
Back in those days maybe --
Maybe the records were a little different.
Yeah.

May 8th, back at the Afterhours, testing this tape for an interview with Sam Baby Lovett. A beautiful day here in Kansas City, absolutely perfect day or evening I should say. Now play this back and make sure it's recording all right.
(Playback)

Good evening ladies and gentlemen, this is Art Smith at the Afterhours with an interview with the great Samuel Baby Lovett, the nationally known jazz drummer, and with Charles Crook Goodwin, the very versatile and capable guitarist and vocalist; one of the finest vocalists we've ever had.

This is Side One of Tape Four of the interview and on this tape we would like to get to the interview, truly an excellent outline prepared by Mr. TAYLOR at the Endowment for the Performing Arts, so we'll start with the very first question that Mr. Taylor has prepared for us.
Now Baby and Crook, over the years, how much of your repertoire was pop tunes, standards or originals and on the originals that you may have played over the years, who wrote these originals?
Well, I would say Jesse Stone for one, the originals.
Jesse Stone, what did he write, Baby?
Now, I forget the name of the numbers, originals,
most of the original numbers I played were from for Jesse Stone.
WELL now, what band was that?
George Lee.
George Lee, and what did Jesse play, what was his instrument?
Piano.
Piano.
He was a piano player.
He was quite a writer. Can you think of any of the numbers that he wrote?
Well, not offhand I can't think. There were so many different numbers.
Well, I would guess that over the years, to answer the first part of the question, that you played pop tunes, standards and originals. Just one second, I have to fix this tape.
(Whereupon, a brief recess was taken.)

Now, as with most musicians and bands and band leaders, any repertoire is going to be made up of pop tunes of the day; that is, to varying degrees. With the jazz band the pop tunes are going to be very much in the minority; standards I think we all agree are hit pretty hard, and the originals were all blessed when we get them. Now you mentioned Jesse Stone. Can you mention anyone else writing originals on a band you were on?
Well no.

He stands out in your mind. Crook, perhaps you knew some of the numbers that Jesse Stone wrote and maybe some of the originals. Of course we know, -- I'll take it from there but Crook, what did Jesse Stone write?
He wrote a number by the name of "Idaho".
"Beyond the Hills of Idaho" that Goodman recorded?
That's the "Idaho" that Benny Goodman recorded, "Beyond the Hills of Idaho", which was a big, big hit.
He wrote another number called "WPA".
That's the number "WPA", that Ella Fitzgerald did the classic recording on and the government said they couldn't put it on the air anymore. He was a hell of a writer.

Numerous numbers but those two numbers stand out in my mind because they were both big hits. They were recorded by big stars and there were several more that were recorded. Incidentally now, Jesse Stone is doing mostly writing and arranging in New York. I forget now, I can't recall what company he is with but he is with a very big company.
What kind of a company?
A publishing house, music publishing house, and another person that stands out in my mind as a great piano player that played with Baby and myself was Rosselle Claxton Rozelle Blackston.
Oh sure, Ros. Roz.
A wonderful pianist.
Yeah, he worked in Chicago. He's still working out of Chicago.
Still in Chicago.
He was with Bill Rinehart at Jazz Limited, down on East Grand.

Yes, he graduated from the Chicago University of Music in Chicago. He got his degree there. He taught a little while, he taught music but his eagerness to play took him away from the teaching and he plays now but he -- he composed some numbers. He also composed some numbers for Louis Jordan.
The Tympani Five.

"Five Little Guys Named Moe", that is one of his numbers, and if I'm not mistaken, I think he composed "Claxton Stomp". I think he composed a number by that name, that title, and well he composed quite a few numbers, a wonderful arranger. Both of these fellows, Jesse Rosselle Claxton Stone and Rozelle Blackston were wonderful arrangers and they both went on to great heights in music.

Thanks, Crook, I think we should add that on our band with Crook and myself, our tenor man, Ben Canard, is the composer of "RED Top". Many people think that Lionel Hampton wrote it but Ben Canard wrote it, and also on my band is Herman Walter, the great alto man, who wrote "Fish for Supper" and "Mellow Bit of Rhythm", and Booker T. Washington, the trumpet player, wrote a ballad called "Just for You". So we have quite a few originals right here in Kansas City and original compositions and I think we'll get back to the numbers before this interview is completed.

I would like to ask a rather provocative question that Mr. Taylor wrote here. Did one man sometimes get credit for another's ideas? What do you think about that, Crook? Can you give us any examples of that?
Definitely. Some years back -- back in the early '30s there was a number composed, "Rosetta". Henri Woode, There was a composer by the name of Henry Woods, which at that time was unknown.
Was he a Kansas City musician?
He was around Kansas City. I can't say that Kansas City was his home. I don't think so.
But he played here?
He played here.
What was his instrument?
Piano. He was a wonderful arranger and composer. He wrote a number called "Rosetta" and he wrote another called "Jeannette", which didn't ever make the big time.
Are you speaking of the "Rosetta" that we all feel that Earl Hines wrote?

Right. That's Henri Woodle's number. I was playing with him when he composed that. I was the first person that did the vocals on it, and several numbers he has written that -- well, they didn't hit the big time but he was a good writer, and somehow or another Earl Hines -- I don't know whether he bought the number or whether he just out right took it but he got the credit for "Rosetta" because his band featured it with Walter Fuller doing the vocals and -- but that was Henri Woodle's number.
There was another little dancer here in town that wrote a number that Andy Kirk made famous, "Until the Real Thing Comes Along".
Oh, that was a big hit.

That was a big hit; that was composed by a little fellow by the name of Van. He was a dancer and he played around on piano and he composed -- he got that together and he had some different words and the tune had a different name.
He composed it as the "Slave Song". When Andy

recorded it, it was "Until the Real Thing Comes Along". Phia Terrell, Fay Terrell, one of my very best friends, did a beautiful job on the vocals, and those are some of the numbers that the composers didn't get credit for.

What was the feeling at the time -- many years ago here in Kansas city with the Kansas City musicians about the controversy of who wrote "Mood Indigo"? Many people, including Barney Bigard Bonnie Bigard and Mrs. Bigard, have said that Barney wrote "Mood Indigo" and of course every credit is given to Duke Ellington. What was the feeling or was there any discussion of this years ago?
There wasn't too much discussion. There wasn't too much doubt that Duke Ellington didn't write it --
That's interesting.

-- but I have heard -- I can't -- don't want you to quote me on it, but I have heard that Barney Bonnie did write the song. But in these instances you have no proof unless the man's name is on the number.

Right, right. Well, we're not going to take a stand either way because as Crook pointed out, there is no proof either way. You know, when you mentioned this dancer, Van, that wouldn't have been the same fellow that got Thamon Hayes involved in a little union trouble, would
No.
But this fellow was a dancer?
Yes.

Sometime I'd like to get back to that because you both were on Thamon Hayes' band and we might as well do it right now. On an earlier tape in this interview it was mentioned that Thamon Hayes up and left the band -- left the band business -- music -- and the band came under the leadership of Harlan Leonard.

Perhaps, Crook, you could elaborate on what happened and why Thamon Hayes, who had a magnificent band, who won that big battle of bands, you might try to describe that too. Let's talk about Thamon Hayes a little bit more; the battle of bands that Booker talks about so much and then what precipitated Thamon Hayes leaving the business completely.
Well this person that you brought up, this dancer, we had been to Chicago -- we had taken a trip to Chicago --
The band.
-- the band, this was Thamon's band now.
Now you're leading up -- why don't we do the battle of the bands first and then get back so it will be more in a chronological sequence.
Well, the thing about it, we were -- this band was made up of guys that were out of George Lee's band and Benny ie Moten's Molton's band; Baby Lovett, Herman Walder --
Booker.
No. Baby Lovett, and Herman Walder were out of . . .
Moten's Molton's band.

No, they were out of George Lee's band and Booker Washington, Ed Lewis, Woody Walder and Vernon Page were all from Benny ie Moten's Molton's band. It was four of them I believe. Well, I wasn't with a big band at that time. I was working at a taxi dance parlor on 12th Street and they were flourishing up and down 12th 7th Street; there were four or five of them up along there. I can't name them all but they were there. They had The Avalon, the Beetle, and several more. This is where I came from to join Thamon Famon Hayes' band. Vic Big Dickenson was playing with Zack White in Cincinnati. Vic They sent for Big Dickenson, and Jesse Stone had a band of his own.
Was Baby with that band then?
No, he was with George Lee's band.
George Lee's band.
Jesse Stone had a band of his own. He brought a band here. Jesse Stone, incidentally, is from around these parts.
Well I wondered about the chronological sequence because Baby talked about Jesse writing numbers, you know --
Yes.
-- and he was on that band. Now was this after Thamon Hayes?
This was during Thamon Hayes' band.
Oh, Jesse Stone was on the band and Baby was on the band and that's when Jesse was writing these numbers?
Right.
But it wasn't a Jesse Stone -- oh, I see, okay. It was during the Thamon Hayes time that Baby was talking about.
Right.
Okay.
Well, as I said, I have named most of the fellows in the band --
Right.
-- and --
Of course we'd done that earlier on the interview --
Yeah.
-- but I wanted to get --
But we --
-- to that battle of bands.

I want to get to the root of how this all started. These guys were all thrown together and they said, "Well, we will show them. We will have a great band", and we would go practice eight hours a day just like anybody going to an eight-hour job, and getting ready for this big event that happened once a year, the battle of bands. There were 10 or 12 bands would participate in this --
Where?
At 15th and Versailles. It was the called then Versailles Dance Hall and this was the biggest dance hall in the black neighborhood.
Was this strictly a black audience for this battle of bands?

Predominantly, yes. It was, you know, not a -- it wasn't hardly a mixed crowd but there were a few whites and Chicanos and what have you that would come in but it was -- it wasn't enough to speak of. It was predominantly a black audience.
And this was a big event?
This was a big event. You couldn't hardly stir with a stick in this hall --
It was so packed?
-- it would be so packed and everybody was -- we were more or less the mystery thing. Nobody

knew what was going on. We kept everything a secret. We had beautiful band uniforms, black patent leather shoes, tan shirts, tan ties and white buttons on these tan suits and the band was really sharp.
Well nobody knew anything about this. We were getting ready. We were rehearsing. Jesse STone had somewhat of a book with a --
HIS own arrangements?

--his own arrangements and we had some stock arrangements and some of the -- along at that time we had big stock arrangements, you know, that were supposed to be just like the real arrangement, the charts and everything and he had quite a bit of those, you know.

Well, as we go on, we get ready for this big event this night and well, when the band -- we all walked in together. Well right then, we captured the audience because we looked so swell. We captured the audience right there. You know, it was our show from then on.
You remember that, Baby?
Sure.
You were in that tan suit, weren't you?
Sure, man.
And then when we did get -- I think we was about the fifth or sixth band to play. When we got on that stand it was pandemonium.
You really broke it up?
We played about three tunes and it just broke the house down. The roof caved in and I'm telling you --
Who was some of the leading competition?
There was Benny Moten.
Benny Moten. That was his rejects beating him out?
That's right.
That's one of the reasons they played so well I'll bet, to show Benny what he lost, huh?
Actually I think the rejects played over their heads, really, because the band did sound good.
Who else? There was Moten's band and two or three or one or two of the other leading bands that were competing with you.
Andy Kirk.
Andy Kirk.

Andy Kirk. All the big name bands. It was a band here by the name of Paul Banks. He was there. Well, he had a band out of -- down the road here in Missouri -- Sedalia -- Sedalia Night Hawks, they had about an eight piece band. It was a good little band but --
How about Jay McShann, was he there?
Jay McShann was doing singles then. He
hadn't come up. Jay was very young then. He hadn't started a band of any size.
Was Moten -- was Basie one of the piano players with the Moten band then?
Right, right. Yes, Basie was there and all the big bands were there, you know.
But you guys took it?
We captivated the house. There was nothing there but us.

Well, I know that we talked about Thamon Hayes. As a matter of fact, we talked about Thamon Hayes yesterday so we don't have to go into the unfortunate experiences that the band suffered; however, I would like to
the whole band was fined for working under scale.
Oh, I never heard about that before.
Uh-huh, the reason -- the reason that we were working under scale, the band was hired for 12 pieces. We had picked up Ramsey, a guy by the name of Ramsey was a dancer to front our band. It was a --
Excuse me, Crook. Was that his last name or his first name?
His last name was Ramsey. I can't remember his first name.
And why would he front the band rather than --
Well because --
Thamon?
Ramon?
-- he could dance. We wanted an act in front of the band sort of.
When you say front the band, you mean an act with the band but not really to stomp off the numbers?
No, he didn't stomp off the numbers but he faked as being a director.
Oh, I see.

See, it was popular during that time, the guys -- they weren't actually directors as such but they would get in front of the band and it looked good, you know. Most of them could dance a little bit and it gave a flash to

the band, you know, gave a sort of personality like thing to the band and this was the going thing. Every big band Bus Moten practically -- Bus Moten was fronting Benny's band and playing accordion and there was a fellow from Oklahoma -- I can't think of his name, his name slips me now -- but he was fronting Andy Kirk's band. So we didn't want to be different so we got one.
You got this fellow named Ramsey. Then what happened?
That was a sorry day because we were taking money from each individual in the band to pay his salary.
But your contract called for 12 men and there were 13.
Right. He turned us into the union.
Ramsey did?

Ramsey turned us in and this is gratitude for you. He turned us in to the union and said we were not making enough money but the reason we weren't making enough money because we were taking money from our money to pay his salary.
Well, what did Ramsey figure to win by
I don't know. He was foreign to us, he was from Chicago and we were Kansas City -- most of us were from Kansas City people
Who knew him?
Nobody knew him.
Somebody had to contact -- or well he contacted somebody?
We met him in Chicago when the band was playing in Chicago.
He must have struck up a friendship with Thamon?

Well, he did. Thamon thought it would be a great thing to have him in front of the band. In fact, he stood in front of the band with tails and a high collar and all this bit, you know, just like a big time director and it looked good but we had no idea that he would do something like this. See this was a setback to the band.
So the union accused Thamon, I would guess, of playing under scale, was that the charge?

the music game.
And it was then that Harlan Howlin Leonard took over the band?
Harlan Howlin Leonard took over the band and which his mother-in-law had staked--
Well, did you guys pay your fines?
Yes.

Did you tell him what I did to Ramsey?
Tell us Baby, what you did to Ramsey.
After we found out he was snitching to the president about us working under scale, I hit him in the mouth.
And you weren't the only one; it was Herman too.

I hit him in the mouth because it was pretty tough back in those days and we weren't making any money and he snitched to the president about us working under scale and I asked him about it and he gave me did some big talk and I hit him in the mouth. That was all.
What ever happened to Ramsey, Baby, do you know.
I saw --
No.
Shall I answer that?
Yes.
All right Crook, what happened?
I saw Ramsey about eight years ago in Chicago. He lives in Chicago.
It wasn't when we were playing there? You didn't say anything.
No, it was before then, about two or three years before we went to play up there. I saw him at the DuSable Hotel, which doesn't exist anymore but I talked to him --
In the black side of town?
It was on the --
Southside?
-- Southside and I think it was on DuSable Boulevard but that's right on the Southside of Chicago and --
Tell us what happened?
-- I was in a club there and --
And what was he doing in there?
Just hanging around, and I talked to him, spoke to him. We never did bring up this occasion that he had done us wrong, you know, and took off like a big bird
you know, when the guys got after him. I mean, we run him for about half a block and if he hadn't been a good runner, boy, he would have got hurt.
Well, you remember when I laid that deal on him?
What was that, Baby?
I had a pistol that day and I was mad when I met him up on the corner of 18th and Vine -- 18th and Vine I met him up there, man.
What was this the next day or something?

No, about two or three days after that and I started to ask him -- I asked him why did he do that, you know, to us because I said, 'You were hungry and we were hungry too' and he gave me some big talk so I hit him and then -- I hate to say this but I had a pistol and I pulled the pistol on him, man, he went running down the street so I just let the pistol fall like that. I couldn't shoot him but he was running away from me, you know.
He really got you fellows upset. Well this was your bread and butter --
Oh man, life's blood.
Life blood, right.
Back in those days we weren't making nothing no way.
But you had to live on what you were
making.
Yeah, and then working with a man who would go and snitch to the president.
We had bought his uniform for him --
Yeah.
-- and everything like this, you know, and he didn't have to pay for that uniform. He had to stoop pretty low to go into something like this.

Well, you know, people have often wondered why Thamon Hayes left the band and now it's on permanent record why he did and now we will end Side One of Tape Four and we'll be right back with Side Two of Tape Four of the interview with Samuel Baby Lovett by Art Smith, with the very, very able assistance of Crook Goodwin.

"Describe the change of solo improvising from playing either with written arrangements or in an improvised, Dixie land style?" Perhaps we could substitute the word jazz for Dixie-land in this particular instance. Baby, tell us about the bands -- I know that you're a very, very fine show drummer, therefore, it's also known that you read very well. Tell us --
Now just --
Go ahead.
-- what would you like to hear about it, Art?
Well, now you had to read when you were with Basie. Tell us about that, when you showed up with Basie, about the charts.

Oh, I had no rehearsal at all. We just had to walked in there and played. If you couldn't read, you couldn't play it so I had to read all the music and everything that was there.
Were the solos written out or were they ad lib? I suppose they were ad lib?
Yeah, the drummer part was ad lib.
How long had it been before that since you had been reading music with a band?
Well, I guess about seven or eight years in Shreveport, Louisiana.
What was the name of the band there?
It was Mac Daniels' band, Mac Daniels, he was a violin player. And I played in that theater eight years in the pit there.
Because playing in pits you had to read?

If you couldn't read you couldn't play because performers come in there and give you -- just put the music out there, the drum parts and everything and they're gone. They don't stay to rehearse. They're gone after they put it out there and it's up to you to play it that night when they come back so that's the way it was. You have to be, I'd say a sight reader to do that too, you know, because some drummers have had some parts where he wanted to go his way, you understand what I mean, and he'd mark it out there and you'd have to look over all of that kind of stuff and I didn't know whether to play that part or not, see, so I just used my own ideas about it.
Would you say that most of the time over Kansas City all these years you were playing without charts? Well, of course, with Famon Hayes you must have had
charts?
Oh yes, you had to read with Famon. Th
Howlin Leonard, charts too? Hanlan

Yes, you had to read because they'd put your drum parts out there for you. You had to read. You couldn't fake that. There wasn't any place in there for your"lick a thang,"lick a thang". You had to read.
Did you ever know a drummer that got in trouble here in Kansas City climbing on a stool and couldn't read?
No.
Or a drummer that could read but couldn't read fast enough?
Well no, I haven't run into that.
Well, I'll address this whole subject to Crook. What do you have to say about this?
Well, during this time you had people that were -- well you might say they were jazz buffs or whatever you might want to call them.
Musicians?

Well they were musicians and some people that were not musicians. They had an act that they would pull on especially a black band because it was a thing where it wasn't -- they weren't too sure that the black musicians could read and they would see a 12-piece band and

these -- well I would call them smart alecks -- they'd go and buy some charts, you know, just simple arrangements. We call them stocks, and they would bring them out on the band and they wanted to pass them around so all the guys, you know -- now this was just a test. It wasn't so much they wanted to hear the number because after they heard the number, it was probably some simple number that somebody -- nobody ever played, you know, but they wanted to have something that wasn't a number that was big on the charts but this number you wouldn't know.
Okay, this is a test, you know.
In other words, you couldn't play this from just having played it before. You had to be able to read it. (Simultaneous talk)
This is what they would bring. I remember once we were on a job and they brought this number, Beguine. "Begin the Begin". You remember that?
Sure. What band was this?
This was Harlan Leonard's band.
Where did this happen, do you remember?
At the University Club.
Here in Kansas City?
On 9th and in Baltimore.
Right.
We were playing for one of the biggest

bankers in town, R. Art Crosby Kemper, and they brought this Bequine number "Begin the Begin". This fellow says, "Mr. Kemper wants to hear this number. Can you fellows play it?" Harlan Howlin said, "It's written there isn't it?" "Yes, it's written here".
Oh, they gave you the charts right there?

They gave us the tune. They brought the tune purposely for this and we spread it on out and gave everybody their part and struck right on into it. We didn't play it perfect because we'd never seen it before but we played it. Everybody was pleased with the way we played it and I might say if we'd had a drummer that night that couldn't read music, which Baby Lovett was our drummer, well we never would have made it because it's the latin had rhythm and you've got to read to play it. Everybody had to read his part or else the whole tune would have been a flop, but I had to put that in because -- but down through the years, you know, until a band gets established, you know, you've got a big band, people will try you.

You know, you have people that go along and you know, they -- I mean you had people come up and ask you, you know, "Do you fellows read", you know. Well, you've got a stack of music this high and they're looking at it. Well they, I don't know, are just pessimists or whatever you might call them but
they just -- they don't know much about music or else they could stand off, see, and they could tell whether you were reading your charts or not.
Well tell me, when you were hiring a new man for a band, you gave him the charts and let him read from them to see if he could really read them and read them fast enough?
You would have a rehearsal with him and the rehearsal, you could tell whether he could read or not.

Well, what changes have you seen over the years, Crook, in this thing of reading and playing without charts and anything you can tell us about charts in those days and how they were handled and where you got them?

Well I think now, I think you'll find more musicians reading music now then you did back in the days when guys like Baby Lovett and myself and some more guys came along because actually I have played theaters -- now I played the Gillis Theater here, which used to exist down on 5th and WALNUT in Kansas City.
The one that burned?

The one that burned down and Lovett almost lost his life in this particular theater. There were three musicians there; Harry Swanagan, Baby Lovett and Roland Bruce, who was a great violinist. Harry Swanagan was a great
pianist and the three of them were working in this theater when this explosion came but --
(To MR. LOVETT)
I'm talking about when you were working there?
Well, when I played we had about seven pieces; the guy hired us, you know --
This was a pit band job?

-- for the pit band. You know, we had to play a show. Now this is before I met Baby Lovett. There was a guy there by the name of Larman Mundy, who was a trumpet player and there were seven of us. I can't remember all the names of the other guys right offhand but the proprietor asked us, said, "You fellows read, don't you"? I've got a show to play", and we said, "Yeah". Everybody spoke up, is "Yeah, we can supposed to read. "Bring us the music" Okay, so he did but with the music, when he brought the music he brought us a little story.

He said, "The only reason I'm asking you fellows this is because you have a -- you guys look nice and everything but I have had bands to come in this place that couldn't read a note and believe me, they were some of the greatest musicians I've ever heard and how they played without reading music I don't know".
I said, "Well this is a gift people have, you know", and we played the show there. It went over nice and we stayed
there about three weeks playing the show but these are some things and these are changes in music. Well now, you know, I don't think the same thing prevails now. I mean in music.

I notice I run across fellows that can't read, you know, some guys playing rock and roll or country western or what have you, you know, but you find more people I think reading music and I think their opportunities are greater and when I was coming along, well I think you could take lessons for $.50, you know. The same lessons you pay $5.00 for now for half an hour. They were $.50 and you'd get a whole hour and well you couldn't find the $.50.

If you were poor, you know, you just had to do the best you could. There are so many self-taught musicians that came along then. One of the greatest ones I think -- we've mentioned him several times; Emil Williams. He was more or less a self-taught musician and he could take songs like "Rhapsody in Blue" and all those big, heavy numbers. I think "Rhapsody in Blue" had about 32 pages and I was working with him, just the, with just the two of us. I was singing and playing the guitar and he was playing piano and he went to town and bought Rhapsody in Blue and don't you know I've never heard it rendered more beautifully.
He would never play it on a job, not 32 pages because that would take the night but he would just play different -- maybe a couple of pages, a couple of movements tonight,

you know, just to let the people hear, you know, that 'Yeah, I'm not just sitting here. My ear is not the only thing that's working. My fingers and my brain works too'. Bring out the point that, 'I do read music'.

But over the years it probably hasn't changed that much. You see, the way the suggestion is to describe the change of solo improvising and I doubt that that's changed at all and I think arrangers, especially when they trust the ability of an individual to ad lib the solos, and they were doing that years ago too, were they not?

My first recognition of a change in solos was -- say trombone, trumpet or saxophone or whatever, woodwind or brass, I noticed a trend back in the early '30s where they began to insert chords and make the musician other than guitar or banjo or piano, they were more chord conscious you know.
I mean, like --
Well this is throughout the arrangement, you mean?
The arrangement --
It had nothing to do with the solo necessarily?
Yes.
Oh.
I'm coming to that. The arranger, I

think that Jesse Stone would write -- instead of writing you out a piano solo, he would write, say just to pick a chord say G7, C7 or A7 or whatever that was going along with this tune and he would just write the chords out for the saxophone or the trumpet or whatever and he would run -- he could just run these chords and this was a sort of lesson to a musician along with, you know -- because most guys that I played with then, they studied but they didn't study chords.

If a guy didn't play an instrument where he had to use chords, well, you know -- in fact, he was playing them but he didn't know what he was playing because he didn't study them. See, Jesse would write, you know, a chord simple symbol for an eight-bar solo for a soloist.
Well that became very popular to write like that, did it not?
Yes.

Like Basie wrote his arrangements all on chords, the keys and the notes were not the important thing. And Well of course I mean jazz is built on chords as well -- but my opinions aren't what they want in Washington but I think -- as you say -- that development -- in other words prior to these chords being notes d by people like Jesse Stone, were the arrangements written out note for note all the time?
Before this time they were. They would write out, you know, a solo, a direct solo.
They'd write out the whole solo?
Some musicians had to have a solo --
But they --
-- but most black musicians, when it come down to the time for their solo, they could improvise. Their ear would tell them, you know, where they were going.
Well, isn't that true today of any black or white jazz musician who's good? His ear has got to tell him.
Yeah, he's mostly improvising when he's --
When he's swinging with his solo.

Sure, and I think this is the best thing for a fellow. You know, this brings us down to what we call soul. This is a guy playing what he feels. This is a person playing what he feels. This is where the word soul comes from because he is playing himself. He is playing what we call soul.

I'm glad you mentioned that Crook and I'll tell you why. You know, over the years we've been playing together, we've come off -- I would say that practically every number we play is soul. We play it really from the gut and it always infuriates me when I get off the stand and some guy says, 'Can you play any soul music', and we've just knocked ourself out with ten choruses of soul music.
What, I wonder, do people mean by that term soul music when a jazz band is playing with its soul practically every number? This just infuriates me.

Well, I think the answer to that is you take a person that doesn't know music and they don't have music appreciation because they don't know one note from the other. Well they'll hear a word, they'll hear a term and they'll ask for something and if you play it for them, they don't know what it is, you understand what I'm saying?
Yes.
But you'll take some guys, just like I'll revert back to where I was saying about these guys passing the music around for the guys because they thought you couldn't read, you know. It's just a thing.
And you said that more often happened you think to black bands than to white bands?
Right, right because the black man, let's face it, he didn't have money to spend to --
Well at least people didn't think he had.

Well, he didn't have money to spend, his parents didn't have money to spend. I'm talking about the masses of the blacks. There were some fortunate like black Duke, who could get music education, but the average family couldn't afford to send his kid to a conservatory to study
music, 'to study music for what, to come out and play in a jazz band', no, but you take now there's more people going to conservatories.
As I remember, I think it was four or five of Duke Ellington's men that were conservatory men.
Well, what you're saying is today a black musician or a black band would not be tested this way like back in the old, old days?
Not really.
I see. Well that's a good thing right there. Baby, were you ready to say something?
No. You were speaking about soul music?
Yeah.

Well, you just don't have to read to play soul music I can tell you that, because down my way in Louisiana, you can take five or six guys just get together and put them off a truck working somewhere or anything man and they get together and you hear some of the best music you've ever heard in your life; no music nowhere, just from the soul. That's why I say soul music is a wonderful thing.
Well isn't most creative music, and especially jazz music, is played with soul, if that's the right expression.
Soul.
It's just a category that somebody has
developed, calling a certain style of music soul music. I think it's obnoxious, really, you know.
You think so?
Well, soul music, we all play soul music but not under this label, this popular music label type thing.
I'll have to butt in and disagree with you.
We all play soul music.
We do not.
There's some people --
I'm talking about the three of us here.
Oh.
I'm talking about the three of us, the jazz musicians.
WEll, when you said --
Oh no, I'm not talking -- oh no, no.
What I would like for the average person to do --
You mean the average person or musician?
The Joe on the street.
Right, the audience.
If he's interested in music and hearing something great, people that you would drag a bunch of notes in front of them, they wouldn't know one from the

other. I would just say to him, "You tour the South through Louisiana, Mississippi, Georgia, Alabama and all down that way and there are people there that don't know anything about music, it's just God's gift."
That's what Baby was saying.
This is, to them I think, this is where soul comes from because I --
I agree. I couldn't agree more and it's not some label you put on a certain way of playing music. If you haven't got it in your soul, I don't care what you call it, it isn't there.
You're right about that, it has to be in your soul.
And I think jazz musicians, we know jazz musicians who play that way.

Now those guys in New York -- take a guy -- you can take and pass one instrument around to five or six different people and let these five or six different people play the same thing and you'll probably pick one out of there that played this thing that excited everybody around and the other four didn't do it because this person that you picked out, he puts the expression in there that captivates the people.
And it came from deep inside him.
This is it. We call it soul.
We call it soul.

I call it soul too but I don't dig this coming off the stand soaking wet and putting everything into a number and having some cat say as you're heading for an intermission, "Hey, can you guys play soul music"?
Well, this is --
Well you're not playing -- maybe you're not playing soul music.

Well this is ignorance on his part, see, because he doesn't know what the word soul means as applied to music. He's just asking the question, you know, and you could bring the greatest person there to play for him; whether he plays soul or whatever, and this is the reason I think that most people now, I think more than anything that people should educate the kids just not to be musicians -- but just for music appreciation, you know, and you can go --
You mean study music appreciation? Well many schools of course have those courses, Crook.
Right, but I don't think it's expressed enough, you know, because --
Well, it's an elective subject, it's not a required subject.
That's right, but this is the way I started my kid up, you know. I wanted him to be --
And here he is in his next to last

year majoring in music at the University of Missouri. Boy it's a long, long way, isn't it? It seems like yesterday he was banging around on my piano; a little kid playing -- what was it, I forget, I got it on tape years ago when he was a little boy.
I can't remember it.
What about the guys down in Louisiana, man, New Orleans especially. They'd play from maybe eight o'clock to two in the morning and you don't see a piece of music over there. That's got to be soul.
Baby, tell us more about those cats down there.
Oh man, those guys man, they play -- everything they play, man you feel it, everything they play. That's what I call soul, man when you can just feel a thing man, you know what I mean.
That's it, that's what I think it is.

Yeah, when you can feel it, that's soul. That's what we call soul see, and those guys can play from eight o'clock man until five oclock in the morning and you're still shouting so it must be soul somewhere.
Exactly.
Yeah.
Well Baby --
I was reared up under that kind of
stuff.
Right, and of course today there are still some fine jazz bands putting out from the soul.
Well it came from New Orleans, you know that.

Many did, and many came from here and many came from New York but we won't get into that right now because that's -- but I know Willie "The Lion" Smith remembers hearing music at the turn of the century with his father, his father was a quarry worker, and about the time -- I think I am of the school but I think it was a simultaneous thing.

It didn't really all originate in one little city called New Orleans. I think it popped up in New York and Kansas City and Chicago pretty much at the same time. TAYLOR, Mr. James Taylor.

You know, the problems in music that are always with us but the question that they ask is when were they most common, such as, intonation, swing, blend, tempo, poor reading, poor knowledge of changes as such, the bridges, the channels? Were these problems more common in the old days or are they very common today? What do you say, Baby?
I think you should mention that again, I didn't understand it all, I didn't understand that part.
Well, let me put it another way.
Yeah.
Would you say the quality of jazz music as it's played today is better or worse than it was in the late '20s and early '30s?
Well, I think it's better.
Better today?
Yeah, it's better today.
What do you think, Crook?
I think with the intonation and the

quality of the musicians that have had the chance of studying jazz music, more and everything, I think if you ask me, it's better. I'll have to digress some to the late '20s and the early '30s to where, I don't know, it seemed like music for jazz musicians, all of them didn't read good and they didn't work on their tones, they didn't practice tones; that is, whole notes to develop their tone and everything like the musician of today does.

I think they work a little harder at it now and I think they do a better job as to playing jazz. Now this is not to take anything away from guys like Coleman Hawkins and Benny Carter. They were great during that time because the reason they were great, they were students of the music game. They put a lot of time into studying music, which made them top musicians and to this day Benny Carter is still a top musician.

He can take his place alongside with anybody when it comes to jazz music and I think this is what we're faced with now today. The music as it is played now is played by musicians who have had a much better schooling than the musicians back in the late '20s and the early '30s. I think this is where the turnover came where the guys began to think about, 'Well, I should study and not just go on what I've got, talent alone. I should try to develop this talent even greater'.

This even goes into the thing where Charlie Parker came along in the late '30s. I think that to me he was a genius of a musician but, however, he applied himself to music more and I think this is what made him so great and I think today the musicians that are coming along are going to be great because I think they study more; that is, for the most part.

And Crook, wouldn't you say that today and every year there are more and more great musicians to emulate, to copy, to listen to? The early day musicians didn't have too many people to listen to and learn from. Now today there are literally thousands of great jazz musicians that can be heard by the young people coming up, which wasn't true 40 years ago. You only had a handful to listen to, so it's a growing -- it's a snowballing effect which I think is tremendous. Baby, did you have anything more to say on this or should we go to the next question?
Go to the next one.

Right. This is a long one -- question but I'll read it. How have tempos changed over the years? When did certain more difficult keys become widely used? When did you first understand the concept of playing on changes?
Well, as a drummer, Baby and I are both drummers, Crook, we probably don't have that much of a problem. Would you want to say anything to that, Baby?
No, we're out of that.
We're out of that. Crook is in it.
Crook, did you want to say anything about this?
Crook.

Well, I've got to answer that this way. Again I would like to go back to the '30s, the early '30s is when I first recognized that musicians -- well I might call them horn blowers and that would take in saxophone and brass and they would -- we would be having a jam session and we would -- well possibly some person would come along that didn't think -- we didn't think he could blow so well and we would immediately speak about -- well these are musicians that understood their instruments pretty well and they could improvise pretty well and also could read pretty well -- so they would, you know, you didn't want this particular guy on the stand and the piano player would look over and say, "Okay fellows, let's take a trip through the keys".

Now this means you would start at a high key and then possibly go down or vice-versa. Now each one of these keys would be a half step. See if he started on A-flat, you'd go to A natural and then B-flat, you know, and B natural and you would play this particular song in each one of those keys.
Well, if you wasn't adept on the instrument, well you couldn't cut it, so you'd have to leave, and I think though during the '30s when the -- in the middle '30s I'll say, it
began to change and it began to become each horn blower become more chord conscious because it gives him a wider range to play and to begin to listen to play.
To play on the changes?
Right, and then he began to listen to things that he had never played before and I think this is where your change came.
Thanks Crook. You know Baby, it does say something about tempo here. Have you noticed over the years many tempo changes? Well, go ahead, you say it.
No, I haven't noticed them. The same thing all the time, especially for drummers.
I would have thought so. You're either playing fast, slow or medium or something in between and I guess it's always been that way in the field of jazz.
Especially for drummers.

Yeah, right. I just wanted to get that in. Here is an interesting question prepared by Mr. Taylor at the Performing Arts. I would say here in Kansas City and as you left Kansas City, the differences between the black and the white musicians?
Now assuming perhaps that the white musicians played

differently from the black, was that difference greater than the regional differences? For example, was the music more different in Chicago than Kansas City, the way it was played, and the differences in the way white and black musicians played? I hope I've made that question clear.
Can I answer this?
Crook Goodwin.

There was a difference. I can remember back in the '30s, early '30s and late '30s, that you would listen to a white band and you could tell this was a white band. You listened to a black band, you could tell this was a black band. There was a distinct difference; now however, the black bands tend to play a little louder than the white bands. I mean the old band and -- but the white bands seemed to me wanted to play what the black bands were playing.

I would notice this because I noticed being here in Kansas City, which was a center for most bands to come through on the circuit or two or three circuits here, they'd come and play the big theaters here. Well, they would all -- all the white musicians mostly would come out where the black musicians were and I think this --
Well, that's always interesting and I often wondered and I'm going to ask you, do black musicians ever go where the white musicians were to hear anything they
were doing; not only here in Kansas City but other cities?
Very seldom, very seldom.
I suppose one reason was they weren't welcome in a white room?

That's right, see, but I have noticed since I first started in music that the bulk of the white musicians would come out to where -- if there was a good black band, they would come out and I noticed oh back in those days well, you know, when you'd wear these stiff cuffs --
Detachable cuffs.
-- the arrangers would come out and they would hear things that the black musicians were playing and they would write down on their cuff, you know, the different things.
When I was a boy growing up in Boston we always felt that jazz, to be really good, had to be played by black musicians, to be really good.
Well, this was the case back in the '30s --
and 40s.
-- and the early '40s but --

Of course I realize now that there are a tremendous number of white musicians playing terrific jazz music and there always has been but there was always a feeling in those days that if it was jazz it had to be by black
musicians.

Well it more or less started from the black musicians because it's a thing between the blues and oh -- and just -- well you can -- it's just a combination of music, you know; what you might call pop music, blues and I think that --
Shall we say that there was a soul factor added to it?
Right. I think that this was because the black man always had some worries, you know.
He lived the blues?
He lived the blues.

That's right.

Were the differences between two black bands greater who were playing in different parts of the country or were they greater between a black band and a white band? That's the way this question is; here at home, for example.
Well --

Yeah.

There had to be something in Kansas City that these musicians wanted. I remember that the great King Oliver was here and this was on his waning days. The days he Betsy was going out, but he did try to establish a band here. It was a band of seven or eight pieces he tried to start here back in the late '30s, and I don't think it was too successful, for the fact that I don't think he got the bookings that he wanted, you know.
Well, we mentioned that yesterday --
Yes.
-- and that must have been after his New York trip, coming back probably on his way to New Orleans?
Yes, right.
Well, I think to summarize -- Baby, did you have anything to say on this?
No, no.

WELL to summarize on this question then, the difference between black and white musicians was probably greater than the difference between a band in one part of the country, black, and a black band 3,000 miles away. In other words --
Right.
-- I would have thought so, but the question was a good one. Baby, what older musicians did you pattern your music after?
You mean my drumming?
Yeah, your drumming, right.

Well, I don't know of any; only my brother. You know my brother was a drummer and he was a great drummer and I used to watch him play all the time. See, that's where I learned -- that's the way I learned drums, from my brother.
Well you were fortunate you had your
brother but if no older drummers influenced you, what about younger drummers?
Well, younger drummers, I don't know. I just -- just from my own ideas about playing drums you know. You notice right now, I don't copy after anybody.
Well --
I try to be just a little bit -- just to have something a little bit different from the other drummers, you understand?
Well, you do have.
It might be rotten but it's different, I'll put it that way.

Right. I wasn't talking about copying but there are certain drummers that I'm sure influence us; maybe not the same ones and I'm sure there are guitarists that have influenced Crook and vocalists that had influenced him.
Well, I'll tell you now, Buddy Rich is my drummer. I like his playing, yeah, Buddy Rich.
Well -- of course -- but of course there was nobody that you really --
And Jo Jones, wait a minute, those two are my drummers now.
Well you and Jo are real pals.
Yeah, but he plays.
Well, I know. He stays at your house every time he comes to Kansas City.
Yes.
I think he taught us all how to play cymbals.
Yes, Jo, is the cymbal man but he says I have faster hands than him, that's what he says.

Yeah, well Zutty Singleton always said you were very fast. You know, Zutty speaks so highly of your drumming but he speaks very highly of Sidney Catlett but may God rest his soul, Sidney used to say, "The greatest drummer he ever knew was Zutty Singleton". He learned everything from Zutty. Big Sid.
Yeah, Zutty was a wonderful man.

Oh, the last time I was in New York.
Well, I told you where he was living. They tore it down so He was living at the Alvin and then he moved toward Woodward.
I went out to his house.

No, he was in a home -- had a home
now there.

No, unless he was just renting there but anyway he and his wife --
Margie.
-- we went out to see he and his wife. This was in a home. Well I'll say dwelling, just like my home.
Well --
I met him there, you know, and he was understand in awful shape, you know what I mean, just trembling like that all the time man.
How long ago was that?
Last time when I was in New York, last year.
Last year.
Yeah, and he came down to Carnegie Hall, man, and they lifted him up on the bandstand so they could introduce him, you know what I mean. Pitiful sight, man.
He's a great one.
Yeah.
Crook, do you want to have something to say?
The reason that Lovett was in New

Baby was.

Newport Jazz Festival.
Yeah.

No, we were down in the dressing room, Jo Jones and I, talking to Basie, and this boy -- what's

Oh yeah, but I wanted the people to see me on the stage, you understand.

Yeah. See I didn't hear him. Joe and I were talking. You know, we didn't hear it the first time and the second time he called it, it was too late to go up there. my name called the

-- in the winter and he spoke -- Jo was going somewhere. I think he said Hawaii or somewhere he was going. I don't know, he might not be but I think he's out of the state.

Oh Jo, yes.
Yeah, his wife --

What do you keep in your drum case?
A's.

7 A's.
7 A's, that's a Krupa stick --
Yeah.
Ludwig 7 A's. I like the 10 A, the one that's got Ray McKinley -- used to have on it anyway.
Yeah.
But I guess like you, I keep light sticks too in case I'm playing in a room where it's got to be real soft.
That is right.
But I prefer the 10 A's.

Oh yeah, you have to use brushes.
Places where you have to use them at times.
Right. We've got some gigs coming up where they want a lot of blues and ballads and I'll be using brushes all the time.
Oh yeah, that's better for that.

Yeah, yes.

In the early '30s.

The banjo could be heard in the small or any kind of combo. I remember at times you would go to record and they had no way of muffling the banjo. Most guys didn't know about the -- they had a mute for a banjo that I had learned about almost the time when I was ready to stop playing banjo; but it didn't work out so good and this -- you'd go to record and they would make you turn your back and play into the drapes so that you wouldn't cut through because that A string on a banjo, you could hear it miles, it seemed like. The guitar was a soft and mellow thing.
You could play more melody with it?
You could play more melody and --
You're talking about how many strings now?
Six, six-string guitar, Spanish guitar, and you could -- most singers liked the mellow tone

of the guitar. If you'll notice now, some singers just have a guitar accompaniment and it is a beautiful thing. I think it just began in the early '30s to realize what potential a guitar had as to be in a band because some bands had two guitars and this is the first starting of the guitar coming into prominence with a jazz band.
What is the first starting?
In the early '30s.
In the early '30s?
Yes.
Because it was more melodic, it was not so harsh, not so penetrating?
For a while I doubled on guitar and banjo but that's pretty rough doubling going.
Do you remember a few years ago we were looking for a banjo for you to play, we had to play one of these Roaring 20s scenes? We couldn't find one anywhere, could we or did we find one for you?
Yes.
Oh we did find one. Weren't you and I looking for one?
(Inaudible).
I played banjo with Baby Lovett's Dixieland band several times.

88 Keys
At the (unintelligible).

Thats right.
-- band to go out to Pearson Hall.

I didn't sell it, it just got lost somewhere on the road.
Oh it got lost.
I don't remember (unintelligible) -- it's been so long.
Well that's great. Of course Baby's responsible for my whole band because he introduced me to everybody on my band. God bless you for that.
Thank you.
You know I've never forgotten it.
Thank you very much, Art.

Oh sure.

Yeah.

Oh he was.

Oh yes.
What did you say his instrument was?
Saxophone and clarinet.

Just strictly reading.
No but I mean -- well what was it, military marches?
Well we called it Ragtime.
Ragtime?
Yeah, back in those days.
You know it's awfully hard to find a good ragtime pianist anymore. It's a dying art. Fess could play.
This old fellow that played the other night, what was his name, old piano player, ragtime piano player -- Blake.
Oh Bobie Blake.
Yeah.
Well --
That's ragtime.
-- there aren't that many around. Remember Fess -- Fess Hill, may God rest his soul .
Oh, we worked together for a long time.
Well he played his last date with my band.
Is that right?
Oh yeah. Yeah, Crook was there, of
course. I remember him doing "Three Nickel Rag" downstairs in the Bar and "Greasy Spoon Rag" but it's a dying art, it really is.
Oh yeah.
What do you do for practice, Baby, because I know hopefully we get it working but sometimes we're not working.
Well I use a practice pad.
So do I.
I can do anything I want because your sticks automatically bounce off this rubber, you understand.
Right.
You can make anything you want to.
Well sometime I want you to show me that left hand of yours, that very brilliant left hand of yours.
Well --
I've watched it for years, mind you, but just the two of us, we'll get together.
Well you see Art, I'm an even-handed drummer. What I make with my right I make with my left and I can show you that.
Fine, well we'll get together.
Whenever you're ready I'm ready.
Maybe when we finish this interview.
Okay.

Speaking of teaching and practice, Crook, do you notice any changes over the years in music training? Well, you've covered some of it as a matter of fact a little while ago. What do you do for practice, Crook, on that guitar of yours? You probably sing in the shower to practice with the pipes, huh?

I didn't know that.
I never sing at home. That's a funny thing but around home you take most people, they will sing or hum a tune or something like that but I never do.
Not deliberately, you just don't think about it or just don't feel like it?
I just don't do it.
In other words, unless you're getting paid you're not going to sing for anybody?
It's not that so much. A tune will go through my mind and silently I'll carry the tune along but in practicing on my instrument, okay, I do this.
Do you practice at home?

Yes, but I've never had any vocal training see, and this is just -- well it's God's gift when you can just go and learn a song, open up your mouth and sing and somthing comes out that the people want to hear.
They sure do.
This is a gift. I sometimes look back and wish I had taken vocal training. Maybe -- who knows -- maybe I would have been worse or maybe I would have been much better.
This is possible, you know. It could have hurt what you had.

Sure, but I've had people tell me I go about singing the proper way. Well, I had no way to know. I didn't know the right or the wrong way to sing. I started singing in a nightclub because I always did remember the lyrics to songs.

This is what I want -- I'm going to interrupt you, Crook. Without doubt, your voice -- you're one of the finest voices and vocalists that I've ever heard and we've worked together now for 12 years or more but the most amazing thing to me is your memory of lyrics. You might not remember the name of the room we're playing in, you might not remember the title of a song but once you hear it, once you hear the opening bars, you've got the lyrics.

I can remember so well one night in Chicago when we were featuring a trombone player there and a wonderful trombone player, Jim Bibe; remember he joined the band for that engagement, and his classic solo was "Blue Prelude". Now we had never done that on my band and when your chorus

came for the guitar, you sang it and you didn't miss a word and I've seen you do this over and over again. We get requests for numbers that we've never played together that you hadn't played or heard for 30 years but you remember the lyrics and I think it's one of the most amazing things, very seriously. I've never seen anybody do this. I've never even heard of anybody doing it. What is the secret of remembering lyrics of numbers you haven't heard for 30 years?

I have no idea. I can't answer it. I can't answer that. The only thing I know is it might be that when -- my mother used to sing around the house a lot. She would go by sheet music, she would learn a song. I would be listening because I was around my mother a lot when I was small and I would be listening and I would learn the lyrics and remember them; not thinking I was going to grow up to be a singer. That was far from my thoughts, being a singer or either a musician.

Actually in school in my primary grades, well I didn't like music. I had all kinds of things against music, you know, but a couple of times I wished I could go and hide when we had this elementary music where you had to write down a note and do all this. I'd want to go and hide. I just didn't like music; that is, to learn it, you know, but after I became a teenager, well I got interested in music through
the ukelele.
Oh, I was about to ask how you got on the guitar/.
Well, I started playing the ukelele and I --
Then banjo?
-- became very adept with the ukelele. I could play the melody and all --
Did you have formal training?

No, I taught myself to play ukelele. I bought a little book and I learned the chords and the single notes and from what little music training I'd had in school, well I could go along with this but when I bought the banjo it was a different story. I had to take some lessons because it was a musical instrument. The ukelele was just a little thing you play around with, however, now you can get a lot of music out of a ukelele if you know how.

On banjo, and I had known him since

early childhood. He was -- actually I knew him in my daddy's Leavenworth, home in Kansas and I knew him then as a mandolin player. Limited?
-- it was limited.

Eddie Durham.
Eddie Durham, he was a guy that you picked up on?
Yeah, he's the guy that I sort of patterned from.
On guitar?
On guitar.
How about classical guitar. Do you listen very much to Segovia?
Very beautiful.
I know he is, but do you listen to him?
Everytime I can. Everytime he --

No I don't have.
But you go and hear him or if he's on --
I have heard him several times on tv.
In your opinion, what is the biggest difference between a classical guitar and the jazz guitar? I mean simple now, quick and easy.

Well, the way you play guitar, I think is very beautiful.

Well I would trade everything I know and everything I could learn in the next 20 years for -- just to be a classical guitar player because I think it's -- you know, you see it played. It's a difficult thing to do but guitar is difficult, period.
You would have had to spend your whole life on that.
Well --
No way you could become a classical
guitarist now.
No way, no. There are so many things that I'd have to learn over.
Well you're one hell of a guitarist, that I know and the best vocalist I've ever heard.
Well classical guitar would be my bag if I had started on it when I was very young. See, I was nearly grown when I started into music so this is in itself --
Well this is an interesting comment, it really is, Crook. Well, let's go on with this excellent outline. Yeah, Baby?
Yes.

No. Well anyway --

Yeah.

Yeah.
