Pro rata -- well the dues --
Yeah, four and a quarter.
Well I wouldn't mind paying that.
Well, you see, this --
The initiation would be a problem.
Well, if you want to join now you --
Well you couldn't join -- you know, initiate every local. I wouldn't mind paying --
But you still have to establish residence here.
Yeah, I wouldn't want to pay the initiation of every local I went into.
You had to -- our local here, 34627, is $156.00. It's just the same as joining from scratch --
I realize that.
-- but the only thing you don't pay is the part you pay to the national.

Well, I don't know. Of course these things will change and what we're doing is going to go on, we hope, for a long, long time. We can't possibly cover all the questions on this outline, this excellent outline I will repeat, prepared by Mr. Taylor.

I'm going to ask a question and this I guess will be the last one unless either one of you have something to add. Did musicians -- I guess -- they keep talking in the past on this thing, we won't talk about today -- but did musicians tend to talk about everyday matters; food, drink, lodging I suppose, chicks and whatever, in a manner that might not be understood by the average person and if so, how? This is going back, say, in the '20s and '30s.
A number of things --
All right Crook. Crook.
A number of things I can say like the band, Thamon Hayes' band, well we had a way of talking so nobody could understand but the guys who belonged to the band.
You didn't do this deliberately, it just evolved?
Yes, we did it deliberately.
Why.
Because -- so the outsider wouldn't know what we were talking about.
When you're talking about outsider, you mean a non-musician?
That's right.
A non-musician?
That's right.
Can you give us some examples?
Well, we just made up language, you know.
Do you remember that, Baby?
Yeah, well we used to say chick, you remember.
Well what I'm talking about is things we used to say like being accomplished, you wouldn't know what
we were talking about.
No.
Being accomplished?
That's a woman.
See, we were saying, 'Look at that lady', being accomplished, see.
The language sounds Italian to me.
Well this is the thing we made up ourselves. This was a language, you know, that we started ourselves.
Crook, [Harmon,] Hewlin and I, you wouldn't know what we were talking about, right now.
We could start the conversation -- the three of us, you know, and we could talk here for 15 or 20 minutes and you wouldn't know what we were talking about.
I think I was the instigator of that thing.
Yeah, he more or less started it, you know.
Baby, you were the instigator of this new language; all right, now this is one band, okay, so you had your own thing. Do you think other bands did the same thing?
Definitely, definitely.
Oh yeah.
See, I remember in the early '30s I run into --
Oh, excuse me, Crook, I'm going to interrupt. Would that be one -- when you say bands, are you talking about just black bands or white bands?
I think they all do it.
Okay.
I think they all do it, both black and white because you have a certain bound there where you're not selfish now, it's not that. It's you just want to talk and you don't want --
It was like a club --
Yeah.
-- a private, a secret society?

Yeah, just like in the early '30s, you know, you take a lot of people now, they speak of being hip. Well this goes back to that, you know. I remember when they had what we called the hip dictionary, you know. Well, you know, just like you saying "the phone". You wouldn't say the phone, you'd say the grapevine, okay, you know. They had different names for different things.

Crook, so the answer is yes on that question. I would like one quick question. We don't have too much time left on this tape. Crook, you and I were walking into a room where we were playing one night and you told me
that you could remember when you weren't allowed to go near that room because you were black, some 35 years ago, maybe longer.
What, very briefly, racial prejudice as a musician, band musician in those days -- I'm afraid we don't -- how bad was it, Crook?

Well, it was very bad but you've got to remember the black musician did have some pride. He thought this way, you know, 'Well, if you don't want me in there, well I don't want to play in there, you know'. So it's just that simple. You had other places you could play.
Well you did run into it though?
Oh yes, had a place where I played with your band that 35 years ago I would have had a hard time delivering a package in there.

Yeah, you told me. I get credit for having the first mixed band in white rooms in this city; mixed and I never realized that until the agent at that time, who was Tommy Reed, told me, and you backed -- you confirmed that down at the local because I checked with you to make sure because I couldn't believe that in that day and age, 1961, '62, but you said that's true.
Now Baby, how about racial prejudice with you and make it fast, Baby, because we're running out of tape?
Well I don't have any racial prejudice.
No, I know you don't, but did you run into it?
Oh plenty of times. Around in Louisiana man, it was sharp.
I should have got onto this earlier.
Oh yeah. It was two guys going to the electric chair.
Well Baby --
I want to tell you about it.

Baby, we're going to have to call this the end of this marvelous interview with Baby Lovett, Crook Goodwin and Art Smith. We thank you Mr. Taylor and Mr. Williams for the opportunity to do this interview and we hope that you'll ask us to interview other people at some future date. It's been great.
It actually is time for my drum lesson with Baby Lovett. All we can say is good night everybody, God bless and drive carefully.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)

segments.title: Copyright notice and opening of the Lovett interview
segments.summary: Standard IJS notices, then Art Smith introduces the interview with Baby Lovett, with Crook Goodwin assisting, at the After Hours.

segments.title: Birth in Pineville and the Star Theatre job in Shreveport
segments.summary: Lovett says he was born in Pineville, moved to Alexandria then Shreveport, and spent about eight years in a theatre band there before coming to Kansas City.

segments.title: Eblon Theatre silent-movie pit band
segments.summary: His first big Kansas City job was the Eblon on Vine Street; he names Guy Taylor's pit band, bassist Eppy Jackson and the pianist Scott.

segments.title: Count Basie playing blues on the Eblon organ
segments.summary: After Scott, Basie joined as organist and played blues during a tense silent-film scene; Lovett scolded him and he behaved.

segments.title: Ben Payne Jazzland, the Pompey Room and the Gillis Theatre explosion
segments.summary: After the Eblon he played a Twelfth Street club, the Pompey Room and the Gillis Theatre, and describes escaping an explosion there.

segments.title: Meeting his wife Tilly in Alexandria
segments.summary: He met Tilly in Alexandria, Louisiana, courted her from age 13 and was married 55 years.

segments.title: Pay of $2.50 a night and tips at the Spinning Wheel
segments.summary: Early-thirties Kansas City work paid little; nine to five for $2.50 plus tips, with visits back and forth to Basie at the Reno.

segments.title: Rialto Theatre pit band with Emil Williams
segments.summary: He moved to the Rialto pit band with Emil Williams on piano and violinist Guy Taylor; Smith explains he wants the career in sequence first.

segments.title: Sorting out the chronology and when he reached Kansas City
segments.summary: Goodwin and Smith untangle Lovett's order of bands, Thamon Hayes and George Lee, and settle that he arrived by 1922-23.

segments.title: Living on Tenth Street, buying a house on Olive, never driving
segments.summary: Where he and Tilly lived, that he never learned to drive, and that he travelled very little before 1930.

segments.title: Years with George and Julia Lee, then Thamon Hayes
segments.summary: He was with George Lee about five years from 1925-26, then joined Thamon Hayes around 1931 for about three years, with two Chicago trips.

segments.title: Leading his own band at the Spinning Wheel
segments.summary: After Hayes he led a band with Herman Walder, Booker Washington and Josh Johnson, playing nine to five.

segments.title: Spiked beer and limburger sandwich at the Spinning Wheel
segments.summary: Stories of the Italian owner's spiked beer and a limburger and onion sandwich that upset his wife.

segments.title: Joining Julia Lee and the move to Milton's Tavern
segments.summary: Goodwin clarifies that after Hayes and the Spinning Wheel Lovett went with Julia Lee as a duo at Milton's Taproom on 35th.

segments.title: Twelve years with Julia Lee at Milton's
segments.summary: Just the two of them for over 12 years; he recalls the record King Sized Papa and says the kitty paid them more than Milton did.

segments.title: Splitting from Julia Lee and playing 40 Highway
segments.summary: Julia went solo at the Cuban Room; Lovett formed a band with Gene Carter and Clayburn Graves at the New Forty Inn.

segments.title: Basie's telegram and joining his band in 1942
segments.summary: Basie's booker wired him to join in New Jersey; he filled in for the ill Jo Jones for about six weeks without rehearsal.

segments.title: Art Smith meets Lovett in 1962
segments.summary: Smith recalls Lovett as the first musician friend he made in Kansas City, introducing him to his band.

segments.title: First night in Jo Jones's seat with Basie
segments.summary: He sat at Jo Jones's drums reading the music, opened with One O'Clock Jump before a packed house, backing Peg Leg Bates and Maxine Sullivan.

segments.title: End of tape one side one and start of side two
segments.summary: Smith closes side one and reopens side two, recapping that Lovett has returned from Basie in 1942.

segments.title: Resting and pneumonia after returning from Basie
segments.summary: He rested a long time after the Basie stint, mentions pneumonia, and cannot recall his first job back.

segments.title: His own band at the New 40 Inn
segments.summary: Goodwin places Lovett's band on 40 Highway about 1943; Lovett cannot recall the personnel and was there a few months.

segments.title: Playing Truman's inauguration with Julia Lee
segments.summary: Lovett and Julia Lee were invited to Washington; Smith works out it was 1945 and that they were still together then.

segments.title: How long he stayed at Milton's with Julia
segments.summary: Smith argues the Milton's stay was nearer seven years; Lovett admits his memory is vague.

segments.title: Forming a new band with Josh Johnson after Julia
segments.summary: After Julia left for the Cuban Room he assembled a band with Josh Johnson and Clayborn Graves out on 40.

segments.title: The Sterling Club with Fess Hill and Saul
segments.summary: Goodwin recalls Lovett worked for Saul, the former Reno Club owner, at the Sterling Club about 1947 with pianist Fess Hill.

segments.title: Gaps in work after the Sterling Club
segments.summary: Smith presses for what came after the Sterling Club; Lovett remembers little except that the band did not last and he was off a while.

segments.title: The 88 Keys trio with Josh Johnson in the fifties
segments.summary: He played the 88 Keys for an Italian owner named Martin as a trio with Josh Johnson and Clayborn Graves, into the sixties.

segments.title: Benny's, Bob Ford's, the Holiday Inn and Huck Finn's
segments.summary: Smith and Goodwin help list the later rooms, working with Josh Johnson until his death, up to the closing of Huck Finn's.

segments.chapter: Learning drums and recording on the Coast
segments.title: Learning drums from his brother Bud on a lard bucket
segments.summary: Smith recaps Lovett's life since 1894 and asks how he began; he copied his brother James 'Bud' Lovett on a lard bucket and cans.

segments.chapter: Learning drums and recording on the Coast
segments.title: His first drum set, a Duplex, bought in Alexandria
segments.summary: He bought Duplex drums in Alexandria, with swinging pedals and skin heads that stayed sharp; his later set was a Rogers.

segments.chapter: Learning drums and recording on the Coast
segments.title: Jesse Aiken and the lesson never to brag
segments.summary: Lovett tells how a boy named Jesse Aiken borrowed his drums at the Star Theatre in Shreveport and humbled him.

segments.chapter: Learning drums and recording on the Coast
segments.title: Recording for Capitol in Los Angeles with Julia Lee
segments.summary: He and Julia Lee recorded for Capitol with a small band including Benny Carter and Vic Dickenson.

segments.chapter: Learning drums and recording on the Coast
segments.title: Staying at the Clark Hotel and the Capitol deal
segments.summary: He stayed at the Clark Hotel, only recorded, got a good contract, and Dave Dexter was involved.

segments.chapter: Learning drums and recording on the Coast
segments.title: Julia Lee and Lovett play the Apollo in New York
segments.summary: Goodwin recalls agents wanting Julia to stay; Lovett says the two played a week at the Apollo.

segments.chapter: Learning drums and recording on the Coast
segments.title: The invitation to play for President Truman
segments.summary: Presidential staff heard them at Milton's, a telegram summoned them to Washington, and the Statler held bourbon from the president.

segments.chapter: Learning drums and recording on the Coast
segments.title: Closing tape one and a joke about competing drummers
segments.summary: Smith ends the first session, jokes about both being unemployed drummers, and signs off.

segments.chapter: Kansas City rooms and Piney Brown
segments.title: Smithsonian title page and microphone test
segments.summary: Title page for tapes 2-5 (Washington, June 1975) and a sound test of the microphones.

segments.chapter: Kansas City rooms and Piney Brown
segments.title: Introduction to tape two on personalities and records
segments.summary: Smith says this tape will cover personalities and recording dates and mentions the outline by J. R. Taylor and Martin Williams.

segments.chapter: Kansas City rooms and Piney Brown
segments.title: The Yellow Front, a jam-session room at 18th and Forest
segments.summary: Lovett played there about two years from eight to five with Robert Thomas on trumpet and Emil Williams on piano.

segments.chapter: Kansas City rooms and Piney Brown
segments.title: Ellis Burton, the Yellow Front owner who fed musicians
segments.summary: Goodwin describes Burton as a strict, generous Black owner who cooked big feasts for musicians and let them jam after hours.

segments.chapter: Kansas City rooms and Piney Brown
segments.title: Thamon Hayes becomes Harlan Leonard's Rockets, and the 1936 breakup
segments.summary: Goodwin explains Hayes's union trouble, Leonard fronting the band, the failed Chicago trips and how members split into small groups.

segments.chapter: Kansas City rooms and Piney Brown
segments.title: The Spinning Wheel, the Reno Club and Basie visits
segments.summary: At 12th and Troost Lovett visited Basie at the nearby Reno on intermissions; his band got $2.50 a night, the leader $3.

segments.chapter: Kansas City rooms and Piney Brown
segments.title: The Sunset Club and its all-night jam sessions
segments.summary: Goodwin describes the Sunset with no front-door key, Pete and Merl Johnson in the house band, and visiting stars jamming.

segments.chapter: Kansas City rooms and Piney Brown
segments.title: Piney Brown as big spender who got Black patrons into white clubs
segments.summary: Goodwin says Piney paid for everyone and his money overcame segregation in white places.

segments.chapter: Kansas City rooms and Piney Brown
segments.title: Piney Brown's policy wheels and Little Piney
segments.summary: Goodwin says Piney's money came from policy wheels, backed by Felix Payne, and distinguishes Big Piney from Little Piney.

segments.chapter: Kansas City rooms and Piney Brown
segments.title: Piney Brown Blues and Joe Turner at the Sunset
segments.summary: They discuss the song, Joe Turner singing for Piney at the Sunset, with Pete and Merl Johnson, while Piney paid for parties.

segments.chapter: Kansas City rooms and Piney Brown
segments.title: How Piney treated musicians and how he died
segments.summary: He paid the same scale but stuffed money into musicians' clothes; he fell ill and died on the West Coast.

segments.chapter: Kansas City rooms and Piney Brown
segments.title: Lovett on Piney Brown, Little Piney and the Sunset band
segments.summary: Lovett confirms Piney was loved by all; Goodwin says Little Piney was younger, golfed, and died in Chicago in the early forties. He recalls little of the Sunset band beyond a bass man from Leonard's group.

segments.chapter: Kansas City rooms and Piney Brown
segments.title: Playing Dixieland with Bunk Johnson at the Yellow Front
segments.summary: Lovett played with Bunk Johnson in Kansas City, not New Orleans, in the thirties; Bunk played Dixieland blues.

segments.chapter: Kansas City rooms and Piney Brown
segments.title: New Orleans musicians who go home for red beans and rice
segments.summary: Lovett and Smith joke that musicians from New Orleans always migrate back; Lovett takes them for red beans and rice.

segments.chapter: Kansas City rooms and Piney Brown
segments.title: End of side one and start of side two, tape two
segments.summary: Smith closes side one and reopens side two of tape two.

segments.chapter: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
segments.title: Introducing Bennie Moten and Lovett's pool games with him
segments.summary: Smith turns to Moten; Lovett sat in with his band but was with George Lee then, and played pool with Moten.

segments.chapter: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
segments.title: The night before Moten's tonsillectomy with Dr. Bruce
segments.summary: Lovett recalls Moten and Dr. Bruce drinking and playing pool on 18th Street the night before the operation.

segments.chapter: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
segments.title: Moten's death on the operating table and Dr. Bruce
segments.summary: Goodwin and Smith say a slip of the scalpel, not a heart attack, killed Moten after Bill Saunders brought him back from Denver; Bruce left for Washington.

segments.chapter: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
segments.title: Bus Moten, Benny's nephew
segments.summary: After a recess Goodwin explains Bus Moten was Benny's nephew Iris Smith, a tap dancer and pianist he followed as a kid.

segments.chapter: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
segments.title: Benny Moten's start in houses and Lyric Hall, the BB&D trio
segments.summary: Goodwin recalls Benny as a youth playing piano in brothels, then leading a trio at Lyric Hall about 1922.

segments.chapter: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
segments.title: Moten expands his band and the banjoist Banjo Joe
segments.summary: Goodwin says Lee's six-piece was bigger than Moten's trio at first, and describes Banjo Joe, who stopped for chalk drinks and was fired.

segments.chapter: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
segments.title: Who played in Moten's band
segments.summary: Goodwin names Jack Washington, Harlan Leonard, Woody Walder, Vernon Page and drummer Mack Washington as earlier members.

segments.chapter: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
segments.title: Moten's pay and work in Kansas City
segments.summary: Moten got the best big-band jobs and paid well, with scale then about $6 a night.

segments.chapter: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
segments.title: Basie arrives in Kansas City and takes the piano at the Bluebird
segments.summary: Goodwin says Basie came about 1927 stranded with Gonzelle White's show and surprised Dude Knox's band at the Bluebird.

segments.chapter: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
segments.title: Basie's style and Fats Waller
segments.summary: Goodwin says Fats Waller taught Basie organ in the East and shaped his playing more than Kansas City pianists did.

segments.chapter: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
segments.title: Jimmy Jones, a young pianist at the Yellow Front
segments.summary: Goodwin remembers the young Jimmy Jones as a great pianist who played the Yellow Front.

segments.chapter: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
segments.title: Basie as sideman; Lee's and Moten's the two top bands
segments.summary: Basie scrambled for gigs but wanted Moten's band; Goodwin says Lee and Moten led the town and Lovett joined Lee about 1927-28.

segments.chapter: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
segments.title: How Basie talked his way into Moten's band for Wichita
segments.summary: Basie sat in for Moten, then showed up packed at the record shop and went to Wichita on a cut of others' pay.

segments.chapter: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
segments.title: Fairyland Park and Moten's two pianos
segments.summary: Back from Wichita, Moten played Fairyland Park, the best job in town at $57 a week, with two baby grands and Basie on payroll.

segments.chapter: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
segments.title: End of tape two and start of tape three
segments.summary: Smith closes tape two and opens tape three, asking Goodwin to continue with Fairyland Park.

segments.chapter: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
segments.title: Moten band's first trip to New York and the Apollo
segments.summary: After Fairyland Park the band played New York for six to eight weeks with twin pianos and was well received.

segments.chapter: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
segments.title: The disastrous second New York trip
segments.summary: Goodwin says Moten tried to play the Eastern style the audience had not hired them for, and the trip failed.

segments.chapter: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
segments.title: Moten lets six players go and rebuilds
segments.summary: After New York Moten dismissed six men, brought in Walter Page and Jo Jones, and kept two pianos with Bus Moten.

segments.chapter: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
segments.title: Denver engagement, Moten's death and Basie taking over
segments.summary: They sort out Wichita versus Denver; Saunders brought Moten back, and after his death Basie took over the band.

segments.chapter: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
segments.title: Goodman, Hammond, the Reno Club and later Basie sidemen
segments.summary: Goodwin says Benny Goodman heard Reno Club broadcasts in Chicago and connected Basie with John Hammond. They agree Edison joined in New York and Vic Dickenson joined Basie later.

segments.chapter: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
segments.title: Moten's funeral and legacy
segments.summary: Goodwin describes one of Kansas City's largest funerals, with Hayes's band standing guard, and Smith credits Moten with putting the city on the map.

segments.chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
segments.title: Lovett on Thamon Hayes as leader
segments.summary: Lovett praises Hayes as an honest manager and nondrinker.

segments.chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
segments.title: Why fame eluded the Thamon Hayes band
segments.summary: Goodwin says the band was never in the right place at the right time despite being great.

segments.chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
segments.title: The MCA offer that Hayes's band declined
segments.summary: An MCA man offered booking at low pay until the name grew; several members refused, though Lovett and Goodwin would have gone.

segments.chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
segments.title: Andy Kirk signs with MCA and his band personnel
segments.summary: Goodwin says the MCA man heard Andy Kirk's one-nighter band and signed him; they list Mary Lou Williams, Ben Thigpen, Floyd Smith and Pha Terrell.

segments.chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
segments.title: Never played with Kirk; the St. Louis night with Ben Thigpen
segments.summary: Lovett tells how Ben Thigpen begged him not to show him up in St. Louis, and he got the crowd throwing hats anyway.

segments.chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
segments.title: B. C. Canard and the Four Tons of Rhythm
segments.summary: They praise altoist B. C. Canard, his brother Ben's audition for Hampton, and the Four Tons of Rhythm in Chicago.

segments.chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
segments.title: Why Bunk Johnson passed through Kansas City
segments.summary: Smith and Lovett say Bunk played at the Yellow Front but did not come to stay or look for work.

segments.chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
segments.title: Emil Williams sent for Lovett to come to Kansas City
segments.summary: Lovett says he came alone because pianist Emil Williams, whom he had played with eight years in Shreveport, sent for him.

segments.chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
segments.title: Bunk Johnson sitting in at the Yellow Front
segments.summary: Lovett says Bunk sat in rather than led, was paid, and did not stay long; Lovett never spent time in New Orleans.

segments.chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
segments.title: Lester Young in Kansas City
segments.summary: Lovett only talked with Lester Young in Kansas City, and Goodwin knew him as a very young, learning player.

segments.chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
segments.title: Kansas City as a hotbed for saxophonists and visiting bands
segments.summary: Goodwin says any visiting star could find an equal in Kansas City.

segments.chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
segments.title: End of side one and start of side two of tape three
segments.summary: Smith closes side one and reopens side two of tape three.

segments.chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
segments.title: Lovett on Charlie Parker in Kansas City
segments.summary: Lovett lived near Parker, says he was too far ahead for local players who would not let him sit in, and walked alone with his horn without a case.

segments.chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
segments.title: Goodwin on Parker's style and hiring him at Lucille's Paradise
segments.summary: Goodwin says Parker blended many players' ideas; he hired him at Lucille's Paradise when no one else would.

segments.chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
segments.title: What Charlie Parker was like personally
segments.summary: Goodwin calls him eager, always moving, caring only for food, rest and his horn; Lovett never drank with him.

segments.chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
segments.title: The Charlie Parker Foundation and a Kansas City jazz alternative
segments.summary: Goodwin describes the foundation's lessons and housing with streets named for stars; Smith suggests honoring Kansas City jazz instead.

segments.chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
segments.title: Playing with Jay McShann at Wolf's Tavern
segments.summary: Goodwin worked with McShann as guitarist and vocalist at Wolf's Tavern, and Smith calls McShann a true exponent of Kansas City jazz.

segments.chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
segments.title: Jay McShann's band in New York and Al Hibbler
segments.summary: Goodwin tells how, in the service, a soldier's mention of a blind singer made him think of Walter Brown, not Al Hibbler.

segments.chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
segments.title: Lovett and McShann; Lovett never ran around
segments.summary: McShann told Lovett he wanted him as drummer, but Lovett never played with him and always went home to Tilly.

segments.chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
segments.title: The musicians union party and the Les Brown band
segments.summary: Smith and Lovett chat about the party and the Les Brown band and its drummer Jack Sperling.

segments.chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
segments.title: Goodwin's tribute to Lovett's steady time
segments.summary: Goodwin says Lovett plays like a metronome and will not budge from the tempo.

segments.title: Record dates with Bobby Sherwood, Red Nichols and Red Norvo
segments.summary: Lovett recalls recording with Julia Lee and these leaders, and using brushes behind Norvo's vibes.

segments.title: Three trips to the Coast and Julia's reluctance to leave Kansas City
segments.summary: Goodwin believes the pair could have been millionaires, but Julia loved home; agent Johnny Tomino is mentioned.

segments.title: Dave Dexter and Capitol's record dates
segments.summary: They say Dave Dexter of Capitol arranged the record dates and the sidemen, like John Hammond for jazz.

segments.title: Dexter stops Lovett using brushes
segments.summary: Lovett was made to play sticks only on record since brushes' 'shish' interfered; Smith defends brush work.

segments.title: End of tape three and start of tape four
segments.summary: Smith ends tape three and opens tape four on May 8th, saying Mr. Taylor's outline questions come next.

segments.title: Original numbers and Jesse Stone with George Lee
segments.summary: Asked about repertoire, Lovett says most originals came from Jesse Stone, a pianist with George Lee, but cannot name titles.

segments.title: Jesse Stone's songs Idaho and WPA
segments.summary: Goodwin recalls Stone wrote Idaho and WPA and now writes and arranges for a New York publisher.

segments.title: Rozelle Claxton and Kansas City composers
segments.summary: Goodwin praises pianist-arranger Rozelle Claxton; Smith lists originals by his band members.

segments.title: Composers who lost credit: Rosetta and Until the Real Thing Comes Along
segments.summary: Goodwin says Henri Woode wrote Rosetta, which Earl Hines got credit for, and a dancer named Van wrote the song Andy Kirk made famous.

segments.title: Who wrote Mood Indigo
segments.summary: Smith raises the Bigard claim; Goodwin says there was little doubt locally that Ellington wrote it but no proof either way.

segments.title: Forming the Thamon Hayes band from Lee and Moten players
segments.summary: Goodwin says Hayes's band drew Lovett and Herman Walder from George Lee and four men from Moten, with Vic Dickenson and Jesse Stone's band joining.

segments.title: Rehearsing for the battle of bands at the Versailles
segments.summary: The band practised eight hours a day in secret, with tan uniforms and Jesse Stone's arrangements, for the yearly battle of bands.

segments.title: Winning the battle of bands over Moten and Andy Kirk
segments.summary: Goodwin and Lovett recall the band entering in uniform, winning the crowd, and beating Moten's band, Andy Kirk and others.

segments.title: Ramsey, the dancer who fronted Hayes's band
segments.summary: Goodwin explains the band hired a Chicago dancer, Ramsey, as a flashy front man and paid him from their own pay, making 13 men on a 12-man contract.

segments.title: Union fines for working under scale end Hayes's career
segments.summary: Ramsey reported them to the union; each man was fined $50 and Hayes $500, which took him out of music and left Harlan Leonard the band.

segments.title: Lovett hits Ramsey and pulls a pistol
segments.summary: Lovett and Herman punished Ramsey for snitching; Goodwin later saw him in Chicago, and Lovett tells how he drew a pistol at 18th and Vine.

segments.title: End of side one and start of side two, tape four
segments.summary: Smith closes side one, saying the Hayes story is now on record, and reopens side two noting the 1933 union trouble.

segments.title: Reading the charts cold for Basie at the Adams Theater
segments.summary: Lovett recalls walking in with no rehearsal in Newark, music stacked on Jo Jones's tom-tom; the drum solos were ad lib.

segments.title: Learning to read in the Shreveport pit and reading for Hayes and Leonard
segments.summary: Lovett says eight years under Mac Daniels in the Shreveport theatre taught him to sight-read, and he had to read for Hayes and Leonard.

segments.title: Tests of whether Black bands could read
segments.summary: Goodwin says doubters handed Black bands stock arrangements to test their reading.

segments.title: Begin the Beguine at the University Club for banker Kemper
segments.summary: Harlan Leonard's band sight-read a Latin chart for banker Kemper and Lovett's reading carried it.

segments.title: Pit band at the Gillis Theatre and a proprietor's reading test
segments.summary: Goodwin recalls playing the Gillis, naming the explosion trio of Swanagan, Lovett and Bruce, and being asked if his band could read.

segments.title: Cheap lessons, self-taught players and Emil Williams's Rhapsody in Blue
segments.summary: Goodwin compares lesson costs then and now and praises self-taught Emil Williams, who played Rhapsody in Blue from the score.

segments.title: Chord symbols replace written solos
segments.summary: Goodwin says Jesse Stone began writing only chord symbols for soloists in the early thirties, making players chord-conscious.

segments.title: Written-out solos versus improvising by ear
segments.summary: Before chord symbols solos were written out, but most Black players improvised by ear.

segments.title: What soul means and Smith's objection to 'soul music'
segments.summary: Goodwin says soul is playing what you feel; Smith complains of audiences asking for soul music after a set full of it.

segments.title: Why Black musicians lacked conservatory training
segments.summary: Goodwin says most Black families could not afford conservatory study, so the reading tests fell mostly on Black bands.

segments.title: Lovett, Goodwin and Smith debate soul
segments.summary: Lovett says soul needs no reading, as in Louisiana work crews; Goodwin and Smith agree it comes from inside the player.

segments.title: Music appreciation in schools and Goodwin's son
segments.summary: Goodwin urges teaching appreciation, and Smith notes Goodwin's son is a music major at Missouri.

segments.title: Louisiana and New Orleans players and soul
segments.summary: Lovett says New Orleans bands play all night without music, which is soul; Smith argues jazz arose in several cities at once.

segments.title: End of tape four and start of tape five
segments.summary: Smith closes tape four and opens tape five, continuing with Mr. Taylor's outline.

segments.title: Is jazz better today than in the late twenties?
segments.summary: Lovett and Goodwin say playing is better now because musicians study tone and theory more, as Parker did; Smith notes more models to hear.

segments.title: Tempos, difficult keys and playing on the changes
segments.summary: Goodwin describes jam-session key tests and horn players becoming chord-conscious in the mid-thirties; Lovett has noticed no tempo change.

segments.title: Differences between Black and white bands and who listened to whom
segments.summary: Goodwin says white and Black bands sounded distinct, white musicians came to hear Black bands, and jazz grew from the blues.

segments.title: Regional style differences and King Oliver's Kansas City band
segments.summary: Goodwin says Black bands sounded alike across the country, and recalls King Oliver trying to start a band in Kansas City.

segments.title: Drummers Lovett admired: his brother, Buddy Rich, Jo Jones
segments.summary: Lovett copied no one but his brother and now likes Buddy Rich and Jo Jones.

segments.title: Visiting Zutty Singleton in New York
segments.summary: Lovett saw Zutty Singleton, frail and trembling, on his last New York trip, and recalls him lifted onto the Carnegie Hall stage.

segments.title: Jo Jones sends for Lovett; the Carnegie Hall introduction he missed
segments.summary: Jo Jones invited Lovett to the Newport festival at Carnegie Hall, where Buck Clayton called his name but he did not hear in time.

segments.title: Friendship with Jo Jones and Max Roach
segments.summary: Jo Jones stays at Lovett's house, sent for him to New York after Tilly died, and Max Roach is also a friend.

segments.title: Drum brands, sticks and brushes
segments.summary: Lovett lists Duplex, Leedy and Ludwig drums, plays any sticks, uses 7As, and the two talk brushes.

segments.title: Why banjo players switched to guitar in the early thirties
segments.summary: Goodwin says the resonator guitar was mellow, better for singers and combos, and banjos were hard to record.

segments.title: Goodwin's lost banjo and meeting Smith at a Pearson Hall rehearsal
segments.summary: Goodwin played banjo in Lovett's Dixieland band and met Smith at a rehearsal for a Pearson Hall job; Smith thanks Lovett.

segments.title: End of side one and start of the last side of tape five
segments.summary: Smith closes side one and opens the last side, noting Lovett's Carnegie Hall introduction.

segments.title: Harry Walker taught Lovett drums and reading in Alexandria
segments.summary: His only teacher was a saxophonist-bandleader named Harry Walker, who taught him to read and led a ragtime band.

segments.title: Ragtime pianists and Fess Hill
segments.summary: Smith and Lovett note ragtime piano is a dying art and remember Fess Hill playing it.

segments.title: Practice pad and Lovett's even hands
segments.summary: Lovett practises on a rubber pad and says he plays evenly with both hands.

segments.title: Goodwin's singing and his memory for lyrics
segments.summary: Goodwin never sang at home and had no vocal training; Smith marvels at his recall of lyrics, which he ties to his mother.

segments.title: Goodwin learns ukulele, then banjo, influenced by Banjo Joe
segments.summary: Goodwin disliked school music, taught himself ukulele as a teenager, then took banjo lessons, first imitating Banjo Joe.

segments.title: Eddie Durham and wishing he played classical guitar
segments.summary: Goodwin patterned himself on Eddie Durham and would trade everything to be a classical guitarist like Segovia.

segments.title: Lovett on booking agents
segments.summary: Lovett says agents are all right and often necessary, though some he will not discuss.

segments.title: Relations with the musicians' union and New York Local 802
segments.summary: Lovett had no union trouble, and Smith describes the union man waiting in the wings at the Waldorf.

segments.title: Hayes's band forced out of Chicago by union rules
segments.summary: Goodwin explains the Chicago local limited a visiting big band to a few weeks, which hurt them near the Grand Terrace.

segments.title: Traveling musicians, transfers and dues in the locals
segments.summary: Goodwin and Smith compare transfer rules, ten percent travelling dues and the cost of joining Local 34627.

segments.title: The private slang musicians spoke
segments.summary: Goodwin says Hayes's band deliberately used an invented language; Lovett started it, and 'accomplished' meant a woman.

segments.title: Racial prejudice faced by Black musicians
segments.summary: Goodwin recalls being unwelcome in rooms and Smith's mixed band in white rooms about 1961-62; Lovett says Louisiana was harsh.

segments.title: Closing the interview
segments.summary: Smith thanks Mr. Taylor and Mr. Williams and signs off.
